speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I really cannot give an answer to that question without consulting the officials of my department and probably officials of other departments, and I am not going to attempt to answer without doing so.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.

Administration service-
1. Departmental administration (including advisory committee on agricultural services). $670,015.

Mr. Chairman, just before ten o'clock last night I was expressing my thanks to private members on the government side for the support they had given us in drawing the attention of the minister and the house to the very serious conditions threatening agriculture across Canada. I had not reached the hon. member for Durham, but I want to include him. I wish to thank especially the hon. member for Northumberland because it is most unusual to have a parliamentary assistant take part in the discussion of estimates when cabinet changes are being discussed and an hon. member might expect to be given the nod at some time.
I should like to proceed to ask the Minister of Agriculture to pay special attention to the remarks made on Tuesday, May 8, by the hon. member for Winnipeg North who asked the Prime Minister the following question to which he received the following answer:
Since the government is prepared to subsidize foreigners to build pipe lines, is the government prepared to subsidize Canadians to build the Saskatchewan river dam project?

Supply-Agriculture

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The government has no knowledge of any proposal by Canadians to build the South Saskatchewan dam project.
I have in my hand a letter, not marked private nor confidential, addressed to the right hon. Minister of Agriculture by the premier of Saskatchewan under date of April 28, 1954. In that letter the premier of Saskatchewan refers to the correspondence and discussions which had continued for a long time in connection with the project. The premier stated that the engineers representing both the federal and the provincial governments had reached agreement as to the estimated cost. For the main reservoir and dam the estimated cost was $80 million; for the irrigation system, $35 million; for the power plant, $20 million; a total of $135 million. The premier also referred to the correspondence and discussions about the responsibilities of the federal and provincial authorities. Premier Douglas emphasized again that the province of Saskatchewan does not expect the taxpayers of Canada to have any part in providing power for Saskatchewan. The premier confirmed the discussions that they had previously and came out with the offer for the province of Saskatchewan to pay $73 million and the federal government $62 million of the total expenditure of $135 million.
I ask the Minister of Agriculture to tell the committee whether or not, in his opinion, the people of Saskatchewan should be regarded as Canadians and whether he thinks the discussions between his department and the government of Saskatchewan should not be considered to have been proposals by Canadians. I want to suggest to the minister that he now is in a most important position, and I suggest that he has but one alternative. It is his duty, as I see it, to go to the Prime Minister of Canada and say, "I must take exception to the references you made in parliament on May 8."
Out of a total of $198 million, the federal government is prepared to put up $190 million to build a pipe line, and this pipe-line company is controlled by Americans, who control 83 per cent of the $8 million, which is to go into the pipe line. So the minister should be able to say, if the people of Canada are going to be asked to put up all but about 4 per cent of the $198 million for the pipeline project-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It appears to me that the hon. member is now dealing more with the matter that we shall be discussing later in the session than the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. On looking at the resolutions, I find that there is a resolution, No. 42, dealing with major irrigation and

reclamation projects in the prairie provinces. In the details, I see that there is a reference to the South Saskatchewan river development. Therefore I feel that the hon. member is in order if he wishes to discuss the South Saskatchewan river development under the general item. He might perhaps contribute to more orderly debate if he chose to discuss it under resolution 42. I do express this conviction, that he is not in order when he commences to discuss pipe lines.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I have really nothing more to say about the pipe lines. All I am suggesting is that the Minister of Agriculture has a responsibility to his neighbours and citizens in Saskatchewan in telling the Prime Minister to proceed with the construction of the South Saskatchewan dam immediately.
I suggest that the Minister of Agriculture should have no alternative but to offer his resignation to the cabinet if the government is not willing to meet the reasonable requests that the Minister of Agriculture has made so often in connection with the South Saskatchewan dam. I think it would not be a bad thing for Canada if occasionally members of the cabinet resigned, on important issues such as the issues we had during the war, when Mr. Power and Mr. Ralston resigned, or it the Minister of Agriculture, on a matter that is so important to his citizens of Saskatchewan, would say, "My resignation must be made available if the South Saskatchewan river dam is not going to get the consideration it deserves." That is all I am going to say on the dam at this point.
I want to come back to the general position of agriculture across Canada and I should like to refer to two articles in recent issues of the Ottawa Citizen. In the Ottawa Citizen of April 26 there was a story by Norman Campbell following a meeting of the Anglican synod of this area. The Anglican synod reviewed with a great deal of concern the depressed farming conditions in the-Ottawa valley. Following that the Citizen sent one of their reporters, Fred Inglis, on an assignment to see some of the farmers. In the area north of Renfrew he saw a Mr. Waite, a 40-year-old farmer, near Almonte a Mr. Steele, over at Carleton Place a Mr. Timmins, and then a retired farmer at Hazel-dean. All these farmers told the same sort of story about the price squeeze which is pushing farmers off the farms and forcing them to go to the cities.
When the minister's estimates were under discussion some little time ago he spent some time discussing the lack of accurate statistical information regarding the farm share of the-national income. I agree with part of what.

the minister said but there is enough information available to anyone who wants to seek it to establish firmly that farmers in all parts of Canada are not getting a fair share of the national income. I realize that you cannot establish exactly the number of farmers who depend entirely for their income on their returns from farming and that it is not possible to establish their position exactly to the last dollar, but we have information regarding gross national income, gross farm income and net farm income.
The bureau of statistics has come up with some figures giving the index numbers of the commodities and services used by farmers. They take the period 1935 to 1939 as a base, and on the basis of 100 for that period you find that by 1951 the prices of the commodities that farmers have to use had increased to 230 and by 1955 had increased to 237. There has been a further increase of 3 * 4 per cent in that four year period when farm prices were going down.
If you take the index for farm prices of agricultural products and use the same base you find that the figure for prices received by farmers was 296-8 in 1951 and in 1955 was 226-2. In other words, there was a drop of 24 per cent in prices for agricultural products while at the same time there was an increase of 3-4 per cent in the prices of the things that the farmer has to buy. Between 1955 and February of this year there was a further drop to 218-3 in the prices of agricultural products.
We find that the drop in prices received by Saskatchewan farmers has been even greater than the drop for Canada as a whole. Our prices in Saskatchewan dropped from 268-7 in 1951 to 187-6 or a drop of 30 per cent. Between 1951 and 1954 net farm income for Canada as a whole dropped from $2-1 million to $1-1 million, or 48 per cent, but for Saskatchewan the drop was 77 per cent.
The disturbing feature about this whole business is that while the farm squeeze goes on corporation profits continue to increase. While in the period from 1951 to 1954 net farm income for Canada dropped 48 per cent corporation profits after taxes only dropped 10 per cent, but in 1955, when agriculture continued to be depressed, corporation profits literally shot up. In 1954 corporation profits, after taxes, were $1-2 million; in 1955, $1-6 million or a percentage increase of 30 per cent.
Now, this situation is serious. The farmers of Canada are a very patient and long suffering people. They do not want too much. But they would like to have at least a kind word from the Minister of Agriculture. Surely, that
Supply-Agriculture
is not too much to expect, and yet we get nothing from the Minister of Agriculture or his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce but these bombastic statements that those of us on this side of the house are talking through our hats, that the farmers of Canada have been more prosperous in the last five years than they have ever been in any five-year period before. Nearly every country in the world is up against the same general proposition, but with this difference. Canada is the only country of which I know where the responsible ministries of the government fail to recognize the situation.
In the United States the situation is serious. I noticed an article by Joseph and Stewart Alsop which appeared in the Telegram of March 13 headed, "Farmers Less Prosperous". The article starts out by referring to a speech by an Arkansas senator in which he referred to the decline and fall of the Roman empire. Apparently the language used by the senator could not appear in the Toronto Telegram but the Alsops say:
The decay of Rome quite certainly began when the hardy farm-citizens whose valour had made Rome great, ceased to be able to maintain themselves and their families by farming their small holdings. In hardly more than a generation, over great areas of Italy, the family sized farms were swept away. They made way for vast, consolidated, slave operated, absentee-capitalist holdings, that were the equivalent in those days of what we now call "industrialized" farms.
Then, the Alsops give us statistics which are available in the United States, and which are comparable to Canadian statistics. I shall have something to say to the minister in a few minutes about his ability to make preparations for compiling comparable statistics in Canada. The Alsops say:
The people who are not prosperous are the folk on the family sized farms. They are so unprosperous, in fact, that this nation is virtually beginning to be divided into two nations. A single statistic tells the story. Per capita farm income has now declined to the level of $860 a year, whereas the per capita income of Americans off the farm now stands at the level of $1,922. Farm folk are much less than half as well off as other folk in America.
In Canada the position of our farmers is relatively a good deal worse than the position of United States farmers. I suggest the Minister of Agriculture has failed in performing a valuable service by ignoring these United States statistics and ignoring the fact that the Canadian farmer is in a much worse position than his United States neighbour.
I continue quoting from the article:
If this condition persists for very long, it can produce only one result. All the ambitious, ablebodied members of farm families will do what the Roman farmers did. They will give up the life they have been trained to. They will pull up stakes. They will go to seek better opportunities elsewhere.

Supply-Agriculture
As I said, Mr. Chairman, while these conditions exist down in Dorchester county in New Brunswick, and in Ontario, the Minister of Agriculture says we do not know anything about it. Nobody knows how badly off the Canadian farmer is. The Minister of Agriculture could go to his colleague the Minister of National Revenue who could give him some useful information. The Minister of National Revenue could tell the Minister of Agriculture that of the 601,000 farm families in Canada only 69,000, just over 10 per cent, in the best year the farmer ever had, had enough money to pay income taxes. I ask the hon. member from New Brunswick if he is aware of the fact that in the year 1953 there was not a farmer in New Brunswick who made enough money to pay income taxes? That is the information the Minister of National Revenue provides.
In the same year there were 130 farmers in Prince Edward Island out of 10,000 who paid income taxes. In Nova Scotia there were 110 farmers out of 24,000 who paid income taxes. In Quebec there were 750 farmers out of 133,000, and in good old Ontario there were 11,000 out of 159,000. Coming to my own province I have to say that in the year 1953, the last year for which statistics have been compiled, almost half of the farmers who paid income taxes in Canada were in Saskatchewan. In that province 31,000 out of a total of 90,000 farmers paid income taxes.
They must have been making money then.
Conditions were better, I admit, but Mr. Chairman, in spite of the fact-
That we had a socialist government.

-in spite of the fact that farmers in Saskatchewan who paid income taxes represented almost half the number of farmers who paid income taxes in Canada as a whole, there were just about one-third of the farmers in Saskatchewan who were fortunate enough to be able to pay income taxes. It is peculiar that the members of this house who happen to have cousins or neighbours who have gone west and made good never say anything about the two-thirds of our people in Saskatchewan who have never had enough money to pay income taxes. Those farmers have never been able to come back home and spend a little money to demonstrate to the neighbours that the west is a land of plenty. I am suggesting to the Minister of Agriculture that if he really wanted to give his party a shot in Saskatchewan-
The hon. member for Rosthern had that.

-I mean a shot in the arm, at this late date, he could remove the present leader and lead the forces in Saskatchewan on the ground that if he were the premier of Saskatchewan again they could build the Saskatchewan river dam out of their own resources and regardless of what Ottawa would do.
Apart from the situation I have been discussing, the Minister of Agriculture could get the information that I have given here and which is available from the Minister of National Revenue, to demonstrate that the farmers in Canada are in a position where 90 per cent of them have never had enough income to be able to pay income taxes. Now, that is something that no member representing an agricultural constituency could accept with any degree of pride or satisfaction. While that is happening, companies like international nickel increase their net profits from $29 million to $65 million; Distillers Corporation increase their profits from $24 million to $33 million. All down the line we have the large corporations of Canada in the position where each year is a bigger year and a better year than the year which preceded it.
I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture that he take time off to read what his own department says about agriculture abroad. On a previous occasion I compared the work of his department in agriculture abroad with the work done in Washington. I offered some criticism on the ground his department did not tell us the whole truth and nothing but the truth as the Washington department does. His department is very careful to keep out of print the information as to what farmers get for wheat in the other countries of the world. Washington does not mind telling the farmers that this is the situation:

Why does the Minister of Agriculture not instruct his very able officers to work out the prices producers abroad receive.
I certainly would not report that. As everyone knows, the $1.40 is not correct.
Well-
At Fort William.
-that is the initial price and we are waiting impatiently to find out what the final price will be. Perhaps the minister would also be able to give us the final price for the 1954-55 crop.
Being such a good accountant, you ought to be able to figure it out.

No; the minister has the information, I have not. I would be happy to have the minister say what it is. Certainly, whatever the final price is going to be, the Canadian price is going to be away down compared with the farm prices in other parts of the world. But in this issue for April of this year the department has a very good article on the Argentine, on Cuba, on New Zealand, on the Soviet union, on the United Kingdom and on the United States. The previous one had articles on Australia, the Argentine, Italy, Denmark and again the United States and United Kingdom. Now, his department has access to the same information that is available to the United States, and I submit that the minister should give instructions to his department that when they are giving this information they should tell us the whole story, tell us how badly off the Canadian farmer is in comparison with our competitors.
I am not suggesting, Mr. Chairman, that there is an easy solution for the situation which is so general when all these countries I have mentioned are using public funds to bolster up that sector of the economy that is living in a depressed condition, and when our exports of wheat represent a relatively large percentage of our production compared with the percentage that the United States exports represent of their total production.
I admit very frankly that poses a real problem. The United States can give away every bushel of their surplus production without any serious impact on their economy. I do not think that Canada could embark on a long-term program of giving away her surplus production. I admit those facts very readily.

Time.

The Chairman can call time when it is up. He is always most anxious to watch the clock and I will sit down when my time is up.
They do not like it.

I realize that to a Liberal member for a rural riding who has not spoken, and who is not going to speak on these estimates, this is bitter medicine. I suggest Mr. Chairman, that the Minister of Agriculture should do something about the situation which is reported and which says that there are no figures anywhere to show what the farmer's share of the national income is.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. As the hon. member pointed out just a moment ago, it is my duty to call time and I now advise him that his time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, it is not very often that a member of one party congratulates a member of another party, especially when that party is a bitter rival, but I am going to take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Mackenzie, who has just taken his seat, on turning in what I regard as a superb performance. His speech, from the standpoint of western farmers, is a masterpiece and is utterly unanswerable.
Are you in a position to judge?

I think I am able to judge pretty well; I have been in the game a long time.
I am glad that the hon. member spoke before I did because it will not be necessary for me to elaborate upon these matters which are vital to all farmers and to all farm-representing members throughout this nation.
I will, therefore, direct my attention to another matter, but before I do so may I put this question once more to all members of this committee and to all the newspapermen who will read the reports of Hansard, and to all the people who will in any way read Hansard and become aware of what is going on in this house. What is the answer to the problem which the hon. member for Mackenzie has propounded? Can that problem go on unanswered without spelling utter disaster to Canada? These two questions have to be answered by every responsible member. There are plenty of hon. members in this house who are not responsible, I am sorry to say, and instead of facing facts they try to evade them, they try to make smart aleck remarks that will get into Hansard. They try to minimize the problems, but they do

Supply-Agriculture
not solve these problems by minimizing them or sidestepping them or being dishonest in respect to them.
I think every hon. member in this committee recalls that on several occasions in time past I have advocated what I think probably affords a temporary solution. As the hon. member for Mackenzie has said, no responsible person in Canada would suppose that we can go on producing enormous amounts of wheat and other agricultural commodities which we are now producing and subsidize the export, or the gift abroad, of those commodities. It is easy to see how a country like Uruguay or Chile or some other country in which agriculture probably constitutes relatively a small proportion of the economy might stand the taxation necessary to subsidize their agriculture and their exports abroad. It is easy to understand why the United States with her stupendous industrial and economic strength can stand to do this kind of thing for a year or so; but even the United States will not be able to stand this burden indefinitely. She is indicating that quite clearly by taking various measures to reduce the production and in other ways alleviate the problem which is bearing so heavily on the economy.
Now, what can Canada do? In the first place I would say this: whatever Canada decides upon as a long-range solution, the Canadian people have no show of right in any way to leave the farmer to bear the rap for the unhappy position in which he finds himself because he has done his job too well. Consequently, while we are readjusting our agricultural production by devices which we may deem to be best suited to the situation, there are temporary measures which ought to be taken and which every responsible member of this committee will acknowledge must be taken to take the burden off the farmer so that he can go on living, so that he will not be utterly destroyed.
I have advocated in times past, and I do not hesitate to advocate today, that the solution to the problem in a general way temporarily is based upon storing the commodities on our farms, paying the farmer the price he should receive for the commodity, and making provision for the permanent storage of that commodity on the farm where it can be only a blessing to us, while we take measures which are necessary in cooperation with the farmers, the provinces and every other agency concerned to determine how to reduce our production or to divert the production into some other line.
Before going on with what I have to say may I quote a passage from the pen of the man whom the minister and the Liberal party

generally are quite happy to quote. They seem to find the claims of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture altogether to their liking. Let me quote a statement from the opening remarks of the brief presented to the royal commission on Canada's future economic prospects by Mr. H. H. Hannam by whom the Liberals appear almost to swear. This statement was made on March 5, 1956 and I read from Mr. Hannam's words;
In the light of conditions and problems facing agriculture, we have set down our views in respect to policies which we believe will be needed-to maintain agriculture in a balanced position in our economy
-to assure those families needed to man our farms a standard of living which compares favourable with those performing a service of comparable value to society . . .
That is all they are asking; that is all the hon. member for Mackenzie is asking; and that is all-I am going to say once more, the courageous, persistent and effective fighters of the C.C.F. party-are asking. I do not hesitate to say that these men have turned in a magnificent job this year. I do not hesitate to say in support of my own party that if the C.C.F. group had not been here and had not been in a position to get the floor first, the Social Credit party would have turned in exactly the same performance because the Social Credit party represents farmers who are suffering just as are the farmers in the constituencies from which the hon. gentlemen in the C.C.F. come.
I interrupted the statement at the words "value to society" and I am going on to quote further:
-to enable farmers to adopt and practice soil conservation measures adequate to build and maintain soil fertility as a vital national asset.
I do not think for one moment that the Minister of Agriculture would be out of harmony with those statements. I want to make it abundantly clear that I do not blame the Minister of Agriculture for the difficulties with which the farmers are now faced. The minister is a member of a cabinet representing all of Canada and his voice is the voice of only one member of that cabinet. His will can prevail only to the extent his fellow cabinet members are willing to permit it to prevail. Let everyone judge the Minister of Agriculture in that light. On the basis of what he has already done, what he has already said, and what he is planning to do, I believe he is just as ready to give the farmers of western Canada a fair deal as are we who, like the minister, come from various federal constituencies in western Canada.
I have no use for people who blame others for things which are beyond their control

and who neglect to give credit where credit is due. I do not hesitate to say there is a great deal of credit due the Minister of Agriculture. I doubt very much whether any man in the country could have done any better in the position in which the minister is placed.
I know the minister will not say that he disagrees in any respect with the objectives set down here by H. H. Hannam of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, but the minister must make the very best he can of the very ugly picture which confronts us by reason of the situation in which he finds himself placed.
I wish to have hon. members also bear this in mind. I am as much opposed to the Liberal party as a man can be but I realize that the Liberal party and the Liberal administration represent the whole of Canada. When they draft a platform in respect to agriculture or when they introduce a measure pertaining to agriculture, that measure must commend itself to the people of every province in this country including Quebec and Ontario, which are largely industrial areas, including British Columbia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland and other provinces which have nothing like the problems which face western agriculture.
When we are dealing with this problem let us be realistic, honourable and honest. Let us give credit where credit is due. I am endeavouring to do that. I do not hesitate for a moment to say that if the Minister of Agriculture were free today and if he were sitting in the seats occupied by the members of the C.C.F., he would be saying the same things that group are saying and with just as much vigour, effectiveness and pertinacity.
I now wish to go on with the statement:
Looking ahead: We want a prosperous, perman-mt and stable farming industry.
Is there anyone in this house, no matter where he comes from, who will disagree with :hat statement? There is not one. Certainly ;he Minister of Agriculture is in complete larmony with that objective. Proceeding with the statement:
We want conditions which will be conducive to iuilding a fine rural citizenship-a farming industry ittractive enough to hold its share of the best of mr farm young people.

structure of any nation are those who are born and trained on farms. They are people of sound judgment, sound minds and sound bodies. That is the kind of people the farms have always produced. The more we cut down the normal healthy agricultural population of this country the more we will be cutting down these young people of stable minds and bodies who make up the very core of the nation, who make the great soldiers in time of need, who become the great statesmen, the great teachers, the great law makers, the great preachers, and the greatest of every division in society. The more we turn the affairs of this nation over to people bred in cities-
Hey!

I am not saying anything against the cities; let me continue. This cannot be said in just a few words. The more we turn the affairs of this nation over to people bred in cities where they have no contact with reality, the weaker our social structure will become.
As a parent I have found it very difficult to raise my sons the way I should like to have them raised because being a school teacher and a member of parliament I cannot put them on farms where they would have to get up at 5.30 in the morning and take care of the pigs and cows and do all the other things which ordinary farm boys and girls do and thus gain a genuine contact with reality, the thing it takes to produce anything of value.
The people who grow up away from farms have the tremendous disadvantage of not being in constant contact with reality, and they feed themselves with their own vain imaginings. Consequently, they become susceptible to communist propaganda and false notions of many different kinds. I say once again that if we cut down the percentage of our young people who grow up on farms we endanger the permanent stability of this nation. I am sure that every hon. member in this house will agree with what Mr. Hannam said in the last paragraph on the first page of the brief;
We prefer to see a continuation of the type of farm program which is based on co-operative self help procedures.
Is there anyone who supposes that the Minister of Agriculture is not in favour of hat? Is there anyone who supposes that here is any individual in this nation who is lot in favour of that? I do not think there s an hon. member in this house from any >arty who would not agree that the best oung men and women who enter the social 67509-241J
We all agree with that, but the main question is: How are you going to bring these conditions about in the time in which we live and in the nation where we live?
Once more I say that as a temporary measure I believe the solution of our problem on the farms in large part is the storing of surplus goods on the farm, paying the farmer what he ought to receive for his goods-

Supply-Agriculture
If we paid the farmer what he ought to receive for his farm-stored goods he would be put in a position where he himself could keep those goods instead of being paid for permanent storage, the cost of which payment would probably wreck the nation financially. More especially it would leave him free to go forward producing whether or not We might be able to sell abroad. I submit that this method of farm storing is far better than giving away products to those who might not want them. It is far better than putting products on the market as the United States is doing. They are subsidizing their prices to such an extent that they come into destructive competition with producers all over the world. There are complaints coming from all sections of the world hy reason of what the United States is doing.
We can understand why they are doing it. It is because they have taken over the ownership of these products and are at their wits' end to find where to store them and how to pay the cost of storage while they are finding some way of getting rid of the products. I do not favour that kind of thing for Canada. I am positive that there is a different way to go about it. I have already stated what my ideas are concerning this matter, first on November 17, 1953 and at various times, at least once while we were discussing wheat marketing this year.
May I go on with another little thing which I believe supports my general position. The Ottawa Citizen of Wednesday, May 9, contained this press dispatch:
1 Study stockpile of NATO food, i,Washington (AP)-The North Atlantic Treaty Organization countries are considering creation of a NATO food stockpile plus emergency food reserves in each member nation, mobilization director Arthur S. Flemming disclosed Tuesday. The proposal which American officials view as a possible outlet for. some U.S. farm surpluses, will receive intensive consideration at a meeting on November 15 of the NATO senior emergency civil planning committee.
November 15; the farmers can starve to death between now and then! The very first thing that these NATO planning people will b'e faced with when they sit down around the table will be how they are going to pay fbr these goods. Will anyone pretend that the TIATO nations, most of which have an insecure and unstable economy, can stand the taxation which would be necessary to provide the money with which to buy our surpluses to store in their countries? Will anyone pretend that? That would be a most unrealistic proposal.
1 Then how are these stores to be provided and paid for? If people suggest an international bank, an international agency to create world money to be spent in buying the
IMr. Blackmore.l
products of Canada, then according to our orthodox thinking which nearly all hon. members would rather die than surrender-if such an agency created the money it would feel that it would have to lend it. It could not get it out of its hand unless it did lend it. Tears of despair! Who is going to borrow it from that international agency? How is that person who borrows it going to repay it, when the only way in which he can repay it is either by taxing people who are already taxed nearly to death or by sending goods in repayment, which the international agency would not accept?
I have said enough now to indicate that while this NATO proposal sounds beautiful, it is just as fallacious, it is just as unsubstantial as the sun dogs in the winter sky that we see sometimes.
What, then, is going to be the solution? How are we to provide those NATO people with our surpluses in order that they may store them? I do not propose to go into any detail because everybody in this house can see that the proposal under discussion is illusory, that it is a sham, that it is foredoomed to defeat, that it will be stillborn.
Here are intelligent men. We hear about the "three wise men" who have been appointed to guide the destiny of NATO, one of whom is in this house, but whom I have never heard express any wisdom concerning economic affairs. Would he know how to provide the money in order to supply these surpluses to the NATO nations? If he did know, and if he did advocate it, he would upon his return get into plenty of difficulty with the Minister of Finance and with all the interests in Canada for whom the Minister of Finance speaks.
What I have said on previous occasions, and I am positive that this is sound, is that the Bank of Canada is able to create all the money which would be necessary to buy all the farm products that can be Stored in Canada at prices which the farmer ought to receive. It can provide the money necessary to build the required storage facilities to house all these surpluses. That will nol cause inflation any more than inflation would be caused if some outside nation bought those same commodities with its own money. Wher that money got here we would change it into Canadian money and spend the Canadiar money in Canada, just as we would spenc Bank of Canada money.
I submit that here is the germ of a possiblt idea that offers a way out. I do not thin! there is an hon. member in this house whc will say that the Bank of Canada is no empowered with all the necessary discretion it needs to do just exactly what I havi

suggested. If we should then want to supply some of these surpluses- to NATO nations so that they might store them, then I say that would be an admirable proposal and one which should have been proceeded with long ago. If we are proposing to let our farmers store the goods having paid for the commodities ourselves with our own credit, we can send those commodities over to NATO nations so their farmers can store them instead of ours with no cost to the taxpayer and no danger of inflation of our economy.
The only question we have to ask ourselves when we are considering whether or not the Bank of Canada can create the amount of money I have indicated is simply this: Are there, at the present time enough commodities in Canada and enough producers of commodities to produce all the goods which would be consumed if that money were spent on the goods of Canada? The answer certainly has to be yes because if we have not enough goods to absorb the money which the Bank of Canada, would create we would.not have enough goods to absorb money that might come in from Russia or any other source. That is as simple as A, B, C.
May I suggest in all seriousness, realizing my responsibility and knowing that these words are going into Hansard and may be quoted against me in future generations, that' we should go to work at once to provide an extensive and comprehensive farm storage scheme. Let me indicate for a minute or two the kind of things we could store in Canada. We could store wheat in superabundance. T ask, what could be of greater value than wheat in times of disaster? When war occurs, or acts of nature create disasters, the first thing that people need is wheat, food. Blessed would be the nation-angelical, almost, would be the nation-that had plenty of food to send in time of need. We have an opportunity to put ourselves in exactly that happy state, if we only have the intelligence and the honesty and the vision to see that we have the possibility.
We can produce a superabundance of oats. If we are now producing too much wheat, let us direct our farmers to produce oats', tell them the price we shall pay them, and give them a firm promise to pay them a price just as good as the price they can hope to get from wheat raised on the same acreage. Then we shall get all the oats we could dream of.
Now turn to barley. Barley is one of the most valuable of human foods. We can produce limitless supplies of barley, all that we can produce with our land and our climate.
Rye, a staple food in many countries, is very valuable as a human food and very
Supply-Agriculture
valuable as a food for certain kinds of livestock. We can produce any desired amount of rye and store it. Flax is one of the most valuable foods, and it can produce oils of great value and residues of great value for stock. We can produce any amount of flax we want and store it, and it will remain safely stored if it is kept dry.
We can produce a tremendous amount of beans. We cannot produce as much beans as wheat, because a great deal of our land suitable for wheat is not suitable for producing beans, and the climate is not suitable in many areas, but in this nation there are areas that can produce beans with great success.
The same applies to peas, corn and grass seeds. I shall stop there for a minute or two. Suppose now that we should become victims of a hydrogen bomb attack.
We are now.

Yes. I congratulate the hon. member for appreciating what is going on now. In case we had a hydrogen bomb attack, how much of the present grass land afterwards do you suppose would be producing grass? How much of our grass today would be alive? And what would be the very first thing we would need to restore that grass? Would it not be grass seed? Of course it would. How, then, could we possibly be more provident than by producing great quantities of grass seed-timothy, brome, rye grass, alfalfa-and storing them where they will be safe, on farms in suitable storage?
Many areas can produce sunflower seeds with success. Sunflower seeds are very valuable food, not only for human beings but also for certain kinds of animals. All areas of Canada are not suited to producing honey, but many of them are. I should imagine that rin Ontario you could almost bury the land in honey.
With regard to sugar, I do not think Canadian citizens realize the potentialities of producing sugar in Canada. By building the factories which the irrigated land we now have in southern Alberta would support, we could produce two and a half times the sugar the whole Canadian population could possibly use every year-in southern Alberta alone. In addition, we would take out of production much of the land that is now producing crops that are a burden to us. Why not produce and store great quantities of sugar? It is easy to store. It is easy to build great bins, something like silos, in which factories like the Canadian Sugar Factories of Lethbridge riding store great quantities of sugar. The sugar will remain there, I should think for centuries, perfectly safe.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, representing, as I do-

Before my hon. friend starts, may I say this? I have been looking up the records, and I And that the last speaker had already made a speech on this subject on February 10. I hope that everyone is not going to speak two or three times.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Well, I have not made a speech on this first item of agriculture so far this year. As 1 say, representing a very important and productive district in southwestern Ontario, and knowing that my farmers face problems too, I thought I should like to discuss some of the problems affecting those particular farmers and probably make some suggestions that might assist in solving some of our agricultural problems all the way across Canada.
As has been intimated by practically every speaker who has spoken on this item, except the minister himself, agriculture is finding it difficult to retain its economic position in Canada. Innumerable speeches have been made in this house, as I have indicated. A great many editorials and news items have been carried in our daily newspapers. Briefs from our farmers' union, our federation of agriculture and practically every other farming organization have indicated, as has the monthly review of the Bank of Nova Scotia, that the farm problems are in contrast to business expansion.
It is rather hard for the farmer operating his own farm when he picks up his daily newspaper, looks over the news items, looks over the financial page and sees that Canada is enjoying one of the greatest booms ever experienced in the history of this great country of ours-it is rather hard for him, as I say, when he has difficulty sometimes in even getting the necessities of life, when he has difficulty in paying the interest on his mortgage, when he has difficulty meeting his tax payments, to understand just why he is in such a situation.
Naturally, he wonders what is wrong. Naturally, he is discouraged. Naturally, more and more of our farmers are leaving the land. Particularly, young farmers who have been raised on the farm and who know how to farm are finding that it will not be profitable for them to carry on the business so well set up for them by their fathers. Naturally, it is hard for them to understand these things.
[Mr Blackmore.]
Many of these young men want to be farmers and would make good farmers as the years go on.
Not only are young farmers forced to leave the land. Many young farmers went overseas in the last war and fought for the way of life that they wanted and, when they returned, used their war benefits and gratuities to that end. But what happened? Many have had to leave the farm and go out and get other positions to augment their farming incomes so that they could meet their current expenses of taxes, living expenses, mortgage payments, interest payments, and so on. Hence their farming operations have not been as good as they should have been.
We have had a great many statistics quoted in this house, both from the government benches and the opposition benches, as to just what is the situation with regard to the farmer. Why is there so much talk about the income of the farmer having dropped to such a great extent I do not wish to add to the great statistical haze that has floated around the house practically ever since the opening of parliament, but I want to call the attention of the committee to an article in the Country Guide entitled, "Why the Squeeze on the Farmers?" The article is written by Dr. E. C. Hope and there is one part of it to which I should like to refer that directs attention in a most concrete way to the conditions facing the average farmer. It reads as follows:
Another basis of comparison is net farm income. In 1951, the average net income per farm from farming operations was $3,520. Preliminary calculations for 1955, after taking into consideration the value of the large crop of last year, show an average of $2,524 per farm. Even considering that 1951 was an above normal year for prices, a drop of $1,000 since 1951 is very substantial.
As I say, it is rather hard for our farmers, who have always felt that the providing of food and agricultural products of all kinds was an important industry in this country, to understand why they are being subjected to this squeeze. As the article indicates, there has been a drop of $1,000 in net farm income since 1951 for the average farmer. How many other segments of our economy could, with the present high standard of living, have continued to exist with such a substantial reduction in individual income, whether it be the man working in the factory, the small businessman, the office executive or the worker in an office? There would have been cries to high heaven that the situation be changed and that something should be done.
Of course, I think we all realize that part of the reason for the decline in agricultural income is directly or indirectly due to the fact that in the past few years we have been

blessed with unprecedented crops of grain and feed in our western provinces. It is also partly due to the reason that the government has been very ineffective in competing with other nations of the world in the disposition of our wheat. Canada no longer retains her position as the greatest exporter of wheat and feed grains that she once enjoyed in the markets of the world. No part of the world can live unto itself today, and probably the fact that salesmen from other countries have been more aggressive and more capable of dealing with world situations than our own Canadian officials is reflected in the condition of the entire agricultural industry of Canada.
As I said before, no part of the world can live unto itself today so no part of Canada can live unto itself. The result is that we find that the western farmer, who has been unable to sell and market his products, has been faced with the necessity of turning to other means of getting cash to carry on his operations. This has spilled his problem into other parts of Canada and has had a very marked effect on the income of feeders of hogs and cattle in southern Ontario. In fact, not so long ago the western farmers were advised by members of the government to do that very thing. They were told that they should not try to keep their eggs all in one basket, that they should get into more than one type of farming. What has been the result? I should like to quote from an article which appeared in the Rural Co-operator of March 27, 1956 dealing with a brief presented to the Gordon commission on Canada's economic prospects. The article reads in part as follows:
The brief, prepared by Cecil Belyea, O.F.A. economist, pointed out that livestock production in 1952 increased over 1951 by 49 per cent in the prairies and 27 per cent in Ontario. Though partly due to better 1951 hog prices, the increase in the west was also caused by the above normal grains harvest, it suggested.
Ontario farmers fear the tendency of western producers to feed more livestock when there are large supplies of unsold grain, the brief said. To supply meat for a predicted population of over 8 million in the province in 1975, Ontario farmers will have to depend to a large extent on western feed grains, the brief stated.
I sometimes feel, along with a lot of other members of the house from eastern Ontario, that the western farmer gets all the breaks. He has got his Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, his Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and this year an act was passed by the house making available to him $32 million for the provision of loans on his farm stored grain. I do feel that if the government does not take more definite steps to rectify these mistakes and assist the farmers the depressed condition is going to affect a great many other segments of our economy. In confirmation

of this, I have in my hand an advertisement by the Steel Company of Canada which appeared in the Hamilton Spectator of March 17. In a big headline at the top it says, "Best Customer", and the advertisement goes on to say:
The steel industry's best customer is the farmer. Directly, the farmer as an individual is a buyer of steel and on the farmer's prosperity rests the prosperity of the farm implement business, which is one of the three Canadian industries using the most steel.
We have had indications in the last few days of extended lay-offs by some of the manufacturers of farm machinery and agricultural equipment. Last week the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose put on record figures which indicated that even in Alberta people producing hogs are doing so at a loss. I have in my hand figures prepared for me by the manager of the Arthur district co-operative with regard to pork production in our part of Ontario. These are approximate figures as of February 18, 1956. The cost of a weanling pig is $8. The cost of 100 pounds of pig starter is $4.80 and the cost of 600 pounds of hog grower at $3.40 per hundred is $20.40. Therefore the basic cost of the pig and the feed is $33.20. A fair average selling price was $36.20, making a gross spread per pig of $3. Then there are the expenses directly connected with hog raising such as interest on capital, depreciation on buildings and equipment, veterinary expenses, the normal loss ratio and labour cost. Then in this magnificent sum of $3 which the farmer makes per pig he also has to allow for disease, price changes and general misfortune. This is the situation with regard to hogs and I may say that the same situation exists with regard to cattle production in southern Ontario.
I should like to make a few suggestions as to some things that might be done to alleviate the situation. In that connection I should like to read part of the policy statement of the Ontario marketing conference which was held on March 13 and 14, 1956 by the Ontario federation of agriculture. Item No. 4 of their policy statement is as follows:
To recognize that the only type of government agricultural policy that can be effected is one which is comprehensive and which takes into account all aspects of our Canadian agricultural economy. We recommend that the federal government give immediate consideration to the establishment of a "granary program" involving outright purchases of sufficient western grains to lessen the danger of western farmers marketing their unsold grain through hogs and other livestock. Grain is a more easily stored commodity than meat.
In the same connection I should like to refer to a bulletin issued by the Ontario

Supply-Agriculture
retail feed dealers association in which they indicate that the situation was foreseen. The bulletin reads in part as follows:
The costly situation eastern agricultural interests are now encountering was foreseen by the trade early last fall. As a result of Canadian wheat board policy it was clearly apparent at that time that sufficient stocks of feed grains would not be moved into winter positions to care for the needs of eastern feeders.
In this article the feed dealers also indicate that more feed grain should be shipped during the fall season while the boats can carry the grain at a cheaper rate than that charged by the railway companies during the winter. In fact our feed merchants and feeders are finding a very definite problem in that connection right now. As a result of the late spring, the farmers are having to feed their cattle a longer time in their own barn.
Another situation that has arisen in connection with the farm industry is brought to our attention by an article in the London Free Press which indicates that the farmer gets only 46 cents out of the food dollar that is expended by the housewife when she goes to buy her weekly requirements. I sometimes think that situation could be improved through research. I feel that this government should spend more money, engage more scientists, and do more experimentation in agriculture so that varieties of produce could be developed which would move to the consumers with less processing and less waste.
In that same connection there is an article in the Rural Co-operator of Tuesday, January 31, entitled, "Ask Research":
In addition the federal government will be asked to undertake research to determine the relative food values of all grades of beef including dairy beef carcasses, with a view to improving sales value.
To improve hog quality the Canadian Federation of Agriculture was asked to work with the Canada department of agriculture to determine the type of program required to produce more "A" hogs in Canada.
The farmers should be provided with this information so that they will know the best types of feed to use and the best animal strains to be developed which will grow faster and be ready for market in a shorter period of time, thus reducing their costs of feeding and operation.
In connection with this matter of research I would go along with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Kindersley last week that there should be additional research into the question of combatting disease in farm animals and the control of obnoxious weeds which costs the farmers millions of dollars each year. In connection with this weed study business I do feel that some steps

should be taken to ensure that more effective methods of grading feed grain would be used to eliminate the danger of carrying obnoxious weed seeds from western Canada to eastern Canada, and to improve the types and grades of feed grain being shipped into southern Ontario. Some samples taken from cars that have been shipped to southern Ontario are hardly fit for animal consumption and should never have left the elevators in western Canada.
I feel also that if the farmers of this country felt that we enjoyed a greater diversity of markets for their products they would not be faced with the problem of their products arriving at disposal points when prices are depressed owing to carryovers. If this were the case, farmers could produce more and would have a greater income to carry on their operations. I feel that steps should be taken to get our agricultural products back into the United Kingdom market once more.
In that connection, I should like to quote from a Searle Grain Company report of February 15. This is a little item entitled, "We Wonder Why".
According to a recent press report, a prominent government spokesman after referring to Canada's large world war trade with the United Kingdom in bacon, cheese, and eggs, added:
"But between 1947 and 1950, they cut off every bit of it. I accepted their reasons but I felt a bit put out when they suggested that we should buy more goods from them."
For the life of us we cannot see why we in Canada should be put out when one of our best agricultural customers suggests what is axiomatic: namely, that the interchange of goods is the very essence of trade and that trade cannot flourish on a one way street. Time and time again officials from Britain have suggested-and even as we write the British Prime Minister, now in Canada, is stressing the point-that if Canada wants to do more trade with the United Kingdom she must be prepared to buy more British goods in return. There can be no quarrel with that, surely?
Once more we have found it is not good policy to have all our eggs in one basket. Every year in the United Kingdom there are millions and millions of people to be fed, whereas the United States, upon whose markets we have come to depend, produces practically the same products we do and also has great exportable surpluses. In the matter of trade, the Toronto Evening Telegram of Monday, May 7, contained an article by James
S.	Duncan entitled, "Our Trade With Britain". I should like to quote one paragraph from that article:
Obviously it is to our advantage to develop and extend overseas markets throughout the world. But the British market is especially important to us as its normal requirements are the primary products of our basic industries and as it provides the largest single market for our wheat.

We have been told that we do not enjoy the British market because they do not have the dollars. This article would indicate that there is a possibility that Britain could be provided with these dollars if we bought more of the merchandise she has to offer.
So I feel, Mr. Chairman, that although this government has done some things for the farmers of Canada during this session of parliament through the medium of amendments to the Canadian Farm Loan Act and the Canadian Farm Improvements Act, that is not the answer. The answer is not to make it easier for farmers to get into debt to carry on their operations, debts which they are going to have trouble repaying. The answer is to take definite steps to assure the farmer a profit on the sale of his products so he will be able to enjoy this great, booming Canadian economy. There is another article in the Steel Company of Canada's magazine which is headed at the top, "The Right Price". At the bottom it says:
The right price for Canada, then, must include a profit for investment in our future growth.
Certainly, the farmer is entitled to a profit so that he may make an investment and carry on the investment that has been carried on for so many years by himself and his forefathers. I sincerely hope that this government will give immediate consideration to these and other suggestions so that the present disparity between the farmers' income and that of other segments of our economy may be changed, and that our farmers will once again find a place in the sun. I hope that the small farmer will continue to enjoy a sound financial position-because I feel that he has made, and will continue to make, a very definite contribution towards supplying agricultural products for the use of Canada and the world-and will also continue to be the backbone of our municipal government. After all, the majority of farmers are proud of the heritage handed down by their forefathers who came to this country, built roads, schools and churches and were always ready to take their place in every organization in the community. I feel that every medium that can be used should be used to assure the continuance of this situation.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I should like to endorse the suggestion made by the hon. member for Elgin and so many other members in this house, that the turkey growers be given a more equitable tariff so that they might compete-and this is true of all the poultry raisers in Canada-with the products from the United States.

Mr. Chairman, before the noon recess I was referring to the fact that the farmers welcome a free enterprise system but they realize that under such a system there are economic ups and downs. I was pointing out that where one part of our economy is depressed the other parts must recognize that fact and be ready to assist the depressed part to take the necessary steps to recover its position and in that way bring about a fair return under our present economic system. At noon I was reminded that perhaps I should mention to the house that I can speak from personal experience about the economic position of the farmer, having some direct knowledge of returns from our own farm during the past few years.
The farmers of this country, like other groups, are quite capable of taking care of themselves and in their present position they will formulate ways and means of coming back into their rightful position, but along with other groups they look for and expect responsibility on the part of governments in assisting them to carry out their policies. In the case of labour there is a recognition of the right to organize under our system; in the case of our manufacturers there is the recognition that certain industries need certain types of protection. These are drastic examples of how governments have assisted at various times in our history. I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture and to the house as a whole that the government must be responsive to any suggestions that come from agriculture at this time and which are put forward in an effort to bring agriculture out of its present position.
I was rather interested to hear an hon. member decrying the fact that the sons of farmers are leaving the farm. I think that has been the case with every generation. I do not particularly decry that, as I believe it will work to the benefit of our economy as a whole and of our country as a whole. No individual farm can continue to maintain all of the family raised on that farm. There is a natural movement cityward and perhaps that has a tendency to improve the quality of our city populations.
However, for those who remain on the farm and are playing a vital part in the economy of this country of ours there must be a recognition of their importance.
Statistics placed before the house show that there is decreasing importance of agriculture in relation to the gross national product. Any manufacturer knows that when

Supply-Agriculture
he loses part of his market he goes from a profit position to a loss position. When the manufacturers of this country lose that part of their market which has been occupied by the farmers those manufacturing concerns are going to start showing a loss rather than a profit. Apparently the importance of agriculture in the whole economy is diminishing but nevertheless agricultural purchasing power is of the utmost importance to preserve in order to maintain that profit-loss balance. It is with a selfish interest that we try to assure that that purchasing power is maintained. As I have said, a small reduction in the purchases from manufacturers will reduce their position from a profit to a loss position. This condition will be immediately reflected upon the condition of other workers who are directly or indirectly connected with the supplying of products which our agriculturists buy.
It is easy to put these facts before the committee and many other speakers have done this more aptly than I could, but there is more to this matter than just placing the situation before the committee to be considered. We should urge the minister-I have not heard it said in any speech that first of all the government should be prepared to acknowledge that agriculture is not enjoying the fat living which the government would have us believe it is enjoying-* to admit frankly that there is a problem. If that were done we would at least have some consolation that the government admit that the problem is there and are at least thinking about it. They should give us some indication that they are showing concern rather than just passing it over. If the farmers of this country do not need the government in order to restore them to their economic position, this government may one day need the farrhers.
I think one program which should be adopted, both by agriculture and by the government, is the greater use of "buy Canadian" slogans. There are just as many vitamins in tomatoes as there are in oranges and yet how many of those who prescribe diets suggest that tomato juice be drunk instead of orange juice. There are many other angles that could be developed on a national scale. Leadership in this regard must be on a national' scale as this is something that can be developed only with the leadership of some federal agency.
Another thing which might be done, and this has been suggested already, is to have more research in agriculture. A tribute must be paid to those presently engaged in this and I think both the federal Department of

Agriculture and the department of agriculture of Ontario are to be congratulated upon their approaches to this problem.
But there is one phase of research which has not been fully explored and which I believe would provide an answer to our immediate problem. Our research in the past has been concerned primarily with production. This has paid off because the productivity of agriculture is continually increasing. However, the need now is for research into new marketing methods and new uses for agricultural products. If the same energies were devoted to that end as have been devoted to the other phase I am sure that beneficial results would follow.
Speaking of markets, how much easier it would be for a farmer-I am dealing with the local situation-to deliver his eggs to the county tovyn and sell them there than to pack them for shipment overseas.
Now let us build this country on a home consumption basis, and on that basis I suggest that the Minister of Agriculture had better get together with the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration so that we may obtain an increase in the population for home consumption. It is far easier, I suggest, to deliver your goods to local consumers, if you have the local consumers. He would be helping not only the consumption end of agricultural products but also the productive capacity of the community as a whole.
I wish to make just one final remark at this stage. There have been recent developments to which our attention has been directed and which may have quite a far-reaching effect upon the farmers in Ontario. I strongly urge that the minister have drafted and ready for submission to this house the necessary legislation to take care of any contingency that may result from the finding of the recent reference before the Supreme Court of Canada.

I maintain this government could do something to correct that situation.
My second suggestion is that arrangements should be made by this government for farmers' organizations and co-operatives in British Columbia to buy their whole grain- wheat, oats and barley-directly from the prairie farmer, but through the wheat board. I would not for a moment suggest doing anything to undermine the proper functions of the wheat board. It was established to protect the interests of the prairie farmers, the grain producers of western Canada, and I would not for a moment suggest undermining its over all authority and its work in that connection. In making this suggestion I have the support of a good many farm organizations in British Columbia. It is unnecessary to have this extra burden of costs caused by shipping to the elevators and then re-shipping through the milling companies to the farmer, placed upon the farmer.
We suggest that if this government would make it possible for farm organizations and co-operatives to buy direct from the farmers through the wheat board-it is only a matter of paper work-the farmers in British Columbia would be saved a considerable amount. In doing that the government would only be extending the functions of the wheat board, by not only protecting the interests of the prairie farmer but protecting the interests of the farmers of British Columbia, Ontario and the maritimes. Now, I have dealt briefly with this question. I urge the minister to give consideration to our representations in this respect. I think this situation, in British Columbia and in eastern Canada, does offer an opportunity for the government to take action to improve the economic position of the farmers without disturbing the over-all benefits that are now flowing to prairie farmers from the wheat board, and of course without disturbing any present legislation. That would in the end be to the general advantage of all farmers and the people of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I have always been a little bit slow in speaking on agriculture, but recently I have been fortified by a trip around my constituency and attendance at an agricultural meeting. I have also been fortified by the knowledge that western members, who may know something about agriculture,

do not hesitate to speak on mining in New Brunswick about which, as it was proven yesterday they know nothing.
It is a good job your constituents are making you wake up a little bit. You should have some more meetings.

You can continue coming down to New Brunswick, and you will find out on June 18 where you belong.
Two recent statements have been made about agriculture that are in line with the general tone nowadays, and they were startling to me. First of all, the president of the maritime board of trade said that the Atlantic provinces spend 30 per cent of their income on food products, yet over 70 per cent of those said food products come from outside the Atlantic provinces. Then, the second statement that was rather startling to me came from one of the gentlemen who spoke with most authority at this agricultural meeting to which I referred a minute ago. He seemed to have some knowledge of the tax situation in his area because he said that out of 50 farms, nowadays only 25 of those farms were being taxed for agricultural purposes, but the whole 50 were still farms. Though the statement is true, and I am sure it is, it was simply a case of their still being on the farm, but the agricultural interests for tax purposes had been drastically changed. They had been reduced 100 per cent in this case.
In his opening remarks, the minister made some reference to the situation in Canada generally. I have forgotten exactly what the details were but my impression was that in New Brunswick the agricultural situation was not out of line with the rest of Canada. I am not going into the details but I want to refer to one or two things that were presented to the Gordon commission by the province of New Brunswick two weeks ago. First of all the statement was made that the capital investment in farms in New Brunswick is lower than any other province in Canada. They went on to make the statement that farm incomes in New Brunswick are very low. I do not think they are the lowest, but they are very low. I believe I read in a table of statistics that the increase in farm cash income in New Brunswick has not kept up with the general increase in Canada. It is not really out of line, but it certainly has not kept up.
The only other fact of significance in the report I think is that the changeover that is taking place in farming generally in the country has been much lower in New Brunswick. It is quite reasonable to assume that

In the west, with the concentration of farming, they would be quicker to take advantage of the changes and the modernization.
Now, I ask, what can the government do in this matter? I say that the government should increase its technical aid. This has been mentioned by other speakers. Of course, they could easily step it up in areas such as New Brunswick where the economy needs a little stimulation. This could readily be given through marketing and food growing policies and also in assisting in the erection of additional cold storage facilities. An example comes to my mind, Mr. Chairman. The marshland reclamation project has been completed; at least the main dam in Albert county has been completed. I do not intend to go into the details of that, although I may have several questions to ask when that item in the estimates of the Department of Agriculture is before the committee. However, I do wish to say that so far as general policy is concerned, the government has gone ahead with the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act, and has spent upwards of $10 million in the maritimes on that project. In my constituency we have the largest part of that reclamation project. I think the amount spent there is well over $3 million. I for one have never been as pessimistic as some others about the project. I feel that it is quite an investment for the future, and the government deserves considerable credit for going ahead with it. I mention this to the minister because I feel it is important so far as the government is concerned. The government began the project; the land has been reclaimed. I was out there the other day. There has been some criticism of the way in which some of the contracts have been let, but to me it looks like a fine, commendable piece of work. But what is to be done with the land, Mr. Chairman, now that it has been reclaimed? The federal government must definitely line up a policy. The land is there; the farms are abandoned. There are over 5,000 acres of rich land which could be used for beef growing or for the resettlement of farmers or for the settlement of new farmers from overseas. I understand that the possibilities of growing grain are good there. I leave this thought with the minister today, Mr. Chairman, as one tangible way in which the government could use those lands to step up and stimulate the faltering agricultural economy.
Some forward steps have to be taken in that area. The farmers are watching and waiting. The government, in order to get the continued co-operation and good will of the farmers, must bring forth a forthright, progressive plan for the development of agriculture in the marshland area.
