speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Mr. Chairman,-

If the item is not carried, may I make a short statement to my hon. friend who has just spoken. The arrangement which was made with the maritime provinces, both Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, was that we would build the dike or the dam, as the case may be, the aboiteau and things of that kind, in order to prevent the sea from getting in on the land, but all the activities behind those operations are to be carried on by the province. That is only natural, because the lands and resources belong to the province, and the assistance we give is to keep out the sea, and then the province carries on the other activities behind the dikes.
I am afraid we would require some different understanding from what we have now if we were to undertake the settlement of those particular lands. The understanding at the beginning, of course, was that the farmers who were already there would be encouraged to utilize the land so far as possible by extending down into the flats where they could not operate before, but a land policy is generally a provincial matter.

I appreciate that, Mr. Chairman. It is the word "encouragement" that bothers me. Where is that encouragement to come from? I appreciate the fact that there is divided jurisdiction. I agree with everything the minister said, but it is the word "encouragement that I take exception to. How is that encouragement to be brought about, and who is responsible for it?

I would think the encouragement of settlement is the responsibility of the province. Where they desire us to take some part in it is another question. The whole question as to what the province thinks can be developed successfully is one which they should determine, not we.

I should like to make -some general remarks on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture because, while I agree quite readily with the remarks made by the hon. member to my right who has just taken his seat, it seems to be most difficult to get this government to recognize the fact that agriculture is in a depressed state. That is one of the first problems that we of the opposition groups have to contend with. This government appears to be drunk with power. It seems to be completely indifferent to the conditions facing our farmers from coast to coast.
We of the prairies have from time to time indicated that since 1954 agriculture in the

Supply-Agriculture
prairie provinces has been receiving a continued set-back in so far as its financial standing is concerned in comparison with the general economy of the country.
The last few days four or five members from the government side of the house have risen in their places and indicated that in the provinces of Ontario, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and British Columbia real problems are facing the agricultural producer, and we no longer have the apple polishers of the government's agricultural policies. Whether or not it is the intention of these individual members to make statements in the house so that they can indicate to their constituents, particularly those in the back concessions, that they have taken some opposition to the do-nothing policy of this government in respect to agriculture, and perhaps indicate that they have put forth policies which would assist the farming people in their efforts to maintain a decent standard of living, I do not know. However,
I wish to say it seems very difficult to convince this government that some remedial policy is needed to rectify the conditions facing agriculture today. Just recently I returned from western Canada.

On a point of order, this is the second time in this debate that hon. members from the C.C.F. party have imputed motives to members on this side of the house who spoke on behalf of their constituents, and I think it is about time they were called to order in that regard.

Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of imputing motives to anyone. The members on the government side can always rise in their places and state their ideas and we are very happy to hear them. The unfortunate thing is that on most of the issues facing the country we do not find them too ready to rise except when they wish to condone such actions as took place yesterday when the government was prepared to take immediate action in order to railroad through issues which should more properly be put to the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member will of course realize that his remarks were out of order and perhaps should be withdrawn.

On the point of order, both hon. members have said that the members on this side of the house are speaking only for the purpose of taking their speeches back to their constituents. I say that is imputing motives. I am sure that hon. members on this side of the house speak with a genuine desire to help solve the problems of this

country, and not simply for political purposes, as was suggested by the hon. member.
Mr. Chairman, I never said any such thing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Kootenay East is quite right but the hon. member who has the floor said that he had no wish to impute motives, and I think we can accept that statement.

Mr. Chairman, the important thing is that while agriculture perhaps relatively does not hold the important place in the Canadian economy that it did a number of years ago, it is still the basic industry of Canada and I maintain that the prosperity of that industry will have a direct effect on the entire economy. When it is recognized that there is a total of $9,593 million invested by way of capital investment in farm land, buildings, equipment and livestock as compared with a total of $8,470 million invested in all manufacturing industries, I think it is clear to all hon. members that agriculture does rank as an important industry in Canada. I have never heard hon. members of this house criticize the farmers of Canada in terms of their being inefficient. I might say that the present condition facing the western farmer is largely due to his efficiency. He has been able to produce extremely efficiently and his surpluses bring about the problem which faces him today. He cannot market the large volume of produce he has been successful in growing. I suggest to the government that not only wheat-which is perhaps not fully under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Agriculture-but all farm products are between 20 and 40 per cent under a fair equity price as compared with the farmer's cost of production. That is the number 1 problem facing the western farmer.
When one considers that entire communities in western Canada are dependent upon the prosperity of agriculture, one can readily recognize that today our farm communities and municipalities are in a position in which it is difficult to carry on.
I was talking to some of the leaders of the farm implement industry in western Canada and they told me they have not experienced such difficulties since the hungry thirties. The sale of farm implements and the problem of carrying on efficiently is extremely serious in many cases.
I wish to point out to the Minister of Agriculture that while we have had prosperity from 1945 to 1952-we had in that period some of our most productive years- vie have recurring droughts in the bread basket of the west, namely the Palliser triangle. Our temporary post-war prosperity

has been largely cancelled out by the conditions prevailing in the last two or three years during which farm costs have gone up, and this government has failed in its policy-

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I have in my hand a copy of Hansard dated February 10, 1956. On page 1083 there appears the speech made by the hon. member on that date. He is repeating it today almost word for word. If he does not agree that that is what he is doing I will read part of it to him.

Go
ahead.

Very well.
The reference is to machinery repairs and parts. In that connection I may say that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, as reported in the wheat pool report of January 1956, asks that tariffs be cut on certain items the farmer must buy-
And so on. Then:
The situation in respect of the whole western economy is getting worse. It is affecting our merchants, our retail sales trade and also the livelihood of the people.
. . . In 1954 sales of all farm implements across Canada dropped 38 per cent, or more than $92 million. Even the sales of repair parts were down 14 per cent, an even surer indication that farmers are pressed for ready cash. In reference to Saskatchewan it says: "For instance Saskatchewan sales last year dropped by more than one-half. Alberta's by 45 per cent."
And so on.
The hon. member continues with the same kind of thing he is repeating today. One of the important rules in connection with debates in this house is that there must not be repetition and certainly when an hon. member is for the second time taking up his 30 minutes in committee and thus delaying the passing of this particular item I think he will understand before he concludes why there ought to be closure in this house.
This makes three times the hon. member has made the same speech in this house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: After listening to the words of the Minister of Agriculture may I say I think he made a very good case concerning repetition. Perhaps I should arm myself with a copy of Hansard for February 10 also.
Get a copy of his speech.

First of all, I want to say that I think it is sometimes extremely valuable to have repetition in this house; perhaps it will lead to a conviction on the part of the government to take some action. On the other hand I might say that the statement I am making is not from any notes I used previously and it is a coincidence that there is any resemblance
Supp ly-A griculture
to what I said formerly. The statement still stands, however, that agriculture is today in need of direct action on the part of this government.
I would suggest a number of things. First of all I suggest that something has to be done to rectify the cost price squeeze facing the producers of this country. The hon. member for Kootenay East spoke about the condition amongst the fruit growers in the Okanagan and we listened to an hon. member from the province of New Brunswick state the situation in which farmers in his constituency and province find themselves. For some years now I have suggested in this house some policies which I think would serve as a solution to the problem facing the producers.
Once the producer has done his job of producing efficiently he is frequently completely helpless in that he has no method by which he can receive a fair price for what he has produced. I submit that the responsibility in this field rests with the federal government. Manufacturers are in a position to ask the public to pay a price which will give them a fair return and in relation to the marketing of farm products there is a problem which must be solved by government policy.
In the last few years we have lost the British market and there are indications in the press that our trade with Britain has fallen drastically again this year. This can only lead to a smaller trade of farm products with Britain. I suggest that this government take upon itself the responsibility to find markets for our farm products. In the past I suggested that in this country we produce only one year's normal food supply for our country and for export. It seems to me that we should have adequate storage for grain and other surplus produce within our country so the producers would not necessarily have to take anything but a fair price in return for their produce.
In Canada we have room for the storage of 580 million bushels of grain at various points outside of the farm points. I submit that could be extended into a food and fodder bank. We could have food storage facilities and fodder storage facilities similar to granaries where these products could be stored for any contingency which might arise.
There are other aspects of this problem to which this government has paid little attention. We have a good-neighbour policy with the hungry peoples of the world under which we are attempting to exert western influence and show the people in undeveloped countries that the people of the west are their friends. By this means we endeavour to counteract Soviet expansion.

Supply-Agriculture
In addition to this use of our foodstuffs there is a great opportunity for the industrial use of farm products. I am speaking now particularly of chemurgy. In order to use our surplus foods for other purposes the government should explore that field and perhaps it could come up with some answers concerning the chemurgic use of our farm products.
I was quite interested in something which was brought to my attention recently which indicates that not only is the farmer taking the rap with respect to the tremendous increase in prices in Canada but also the consumer is victimized. One item which illustrates the situation is farm livestock products. Today the consumer is still paying high prices for choice meat cuts. The records of the Winnipeg stock exchange show that the farmers are getting 16 or 17 cents for choice beef.
Then there is the matter of the by-products. Taking the 1935-39 period as an index figure of 100 we find that the wholesale price index of raw hides, including sheep and calfskins, increased from 103-8 in 1939 to 114-4 in 1955. But when these hides are turned into boots and shoes we find that in that same period the index rose from 101-8 to 204-4. It will be seen that while in many cases the prices received by the farmer have gone down the consumer is paying higher prices for the things manufactured from farm products.
I have here an article which appeared in the Journal of April 21 entitled "Why the Farmer Complains" and I should like to read one short paragraph as follows:
D.B.S. states that in 1955 farmers in Canada received 46 cents of the consumers' food dollar, two cents less than the 1949-54 average. But while 1955 retail food prices were 11 per cent higher than in 1949 the farmer received 3 per cent less and marketing costs were up almost 25 per cent.
I just want to leave this thought with the committee, that while the government may be self-satisfied with the rather buoyant economy evident in our industrial, oil and mineral development, we find this great segment of the Canadian economy, and I refer to agriculture, facing perhaps one of the most serious situations since the hungry thirties. I suggest to the government that we still have in Canada the possibilities of doing something for the farmer. There are many old age pensioners living on $40 a month and in many cases they do not have the kind of food they should have. I suggest that some way should be devised to get some of this surplus food into the hands of our old age pensioners and families in the low income brackets. Some

policy should be evolved whereby the standard of living of such people could be increased so that they could buy more of the food which is now in surplus in Canada.
I have investigated some of the policies carried on by the United States government. They have a school lunch program under which school children are given milk and dairy products. The federal government in the United States is undertaking a $5,000 million program to guarantee the farmers a fair price as related to their costs of production. In this country the government has done nothing. It has its defence production program and other development programs but is quite satisfied to leave the farmer out of this prosperity in Canada.
Our farmers gave the war effort everything they had and yet today we find these same people in this price-cost squeeze. Many returned men came back and went on the land but today find themselves loaded with debt. Unless something is done to straighten out this cost-price squeeze they will find themselves in the position in which their fathers were when they came back after the first world war. Those men went on the land under soldier settlement schemes and many of them lost their farms.
There is a definite need for the Minister of Agriculture to meet with his colleagues. I think this matter is just as important as the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines or any other issue that may face this government. I suggest to the government that now that this grain has been produced the farmers should not be forced to sell it at a price which does not bear a fair relationship to their costs of production. Their farm machinery costs and other costs are increasing and they face the possibility of being saddled with debt.
It' is not satisfactory just to pass legislation to give the farmer the right to go to the bank to borrow money on a long-term amortization arrangement. What we want in this country is a more prosperous farm economy. In this house we talk mostly about monetary policies, but there is this other important and nonetheless tangible aspect of our economy. We must give a fair deal to the people on the soil. The strength of this nation has been in the people on the land and today those people are worried. They are filled with apathy. The young people are leaving the farms to go into industry where they can obtain more lucrative employment.
I do not want to delay this item but I do want to impress upon the Minister of Agriculture that he has a real job on his hands to convince this government that they should act. All we have to do is to look at some of the corporation profits that have been made

and the buoyant economy which has been indicated by the Minister of Finance. An article in the Toronto Star of April 19 indicates that profits in 1955 hit $1,656 million, up 35 per cent. But the farmers of this country, the people who are the backbone of this country, find their standard of living is going down. So I do hope that we will have a real answer by the government to this problem which is facing the farmer.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one or two remarks in connection with the points just raised and which I think should be answered. It is suggested that we should have a milk program in connection with the schools such as they have in the United States. Everyone in the committee knows that there are milk boards in every province and anything that is going to be done to put milk in schools must be done by the provinces.
Dbn't pass the buck again.

I have just one short question. The minister made reference to a policy regarding the supply of whole milk to school children across Canada. I wonder if he would

Supply-Agriculture
tell the committee what that policy is and whether the provinces have been made aware of this policy.

We have indicated to provincial officials and ministers who come here from time to time to the conference and advisory committee that has been spoken of here, and others, the investigations we have made in the state of New York and elsewhere as to how the program is carried out. We have suggested we are prepared to consider with any of them any system that they desire to put in and to consider even the possibility of giving some assistance in connection with the obtaining of the kind of machines used there in general practice, where something is put in a slot and a bottle of milk is obtained.
Then the truth is that no definite policy has been arrived at? It has just been considered with the provinces. No actual policy has been handed to the provinces?
A better way to state it is that no province has devised a policy to make use of it.
The federal government has never offered them a policy.
We cannot distribute milk in the provinces. As a matter of fact, they will not let us have anything to do with the administration of milk boards. That is their responsibility, and they take it.

May I
ask the minister whether there is any definite commitment as to the financial obligation that the federal government would be prepared to undertake in respect to the plan he has indicated?
No.
If any province will make a proposition to us that they want it done, we shall submit to them at once what we are prepared to do.

I do not wish to delay the house at any length. I do feel that it is interesting to listen to the discussions and observe the more or less nonchalant complacency of the government and its supporters with reference to agriculture generally. However, I am glad to learn today that the dairy men have learned that there is a new slot-machine policy being established in their interests. It may be of some real help. The minister has not said whether he will supply the slot machines or the milk, but it is something at least for them to hope for in future.
No doubt there have been great changes in agriculture generally, and its importance and place in our Canadian economy. I make

no apologies for mentioning its place here, on the first item, because that is about the only item on which we might be able to make observations as to the position the farmers are in throughout the dominion. That is why those, especially, who do not belong to the government have felt probably they should make vigorous statements at such times and have tried to place before parliament the position of their farmers in their respective districts.
I believe, independent of party, every hon. member in this house realizes the very important place of Canadian agriculture in the life of this dominion. It is true that that place is not as prominent on a percentage basis in our national production as it was a few years ago. In fact, it has changed very greatly. The figures have been placed on Hansard very often to show that the percentage of our whole industrial development has increased in other lines, while today agriculture has only about half the importance on the basis of percentage of gross national production. Indeed, those employed and obtaining subsistence from the agricultural industry are greatly reduced in numbers in view of machinery and other developments. That tends to make some people doubt the importance of agriculture.
Some hon. member this afternoon has used the term that many of us have used at times, that agriculture is the backbone of Canadian prosperity. We have used that term in the past and some of us now doubt whether it is so much the backbone. In fact, at times one would think the back was almost broken by the change in this part of our whole prosperity. The industrial development of our country and the numbers of people employed in our industrial and commercial enterprises in Canada are now increasing much more rapidly than agriculture. In fact those in agriculture, as I have said, are reduced in numbers. But I believe the government, as well as some people such as I have mentioned, seems to have more or less let the chances of agriculture grow more and more haphazard. Policies have been tried of handouts here and handouts there, subsidies and fixed prices, and it is struggling for a solution, but more or less with the attitude that we shall get along all right whether agriculture is prosperous or not.
Now we are beginning to see the effects. We see now that there are already many people unemployed in Canada today and many are looking for other jobs, whether you would call them fully unemployed now or not, because of the reduced purchasing power of the Canadian farmer. In the small towns and villages across this country, farm tractor sales have been reduced very much this

spring. I believe hon. members will find in their respective districts that farm tractor salesmen will tell them that they are not selling any farm tractors where they sold ten last year. In fact, in some districts it is even worse than that proportionately, even to the extent that in some districts the price of the heavy draught horse has increased because the farmers feel they cannot afford to repair their tractors or buy new tractors. That has happened in several districts.
I do claim that we seem to overlook the importance of sound national policies with respect to agriculture. Just as agriculture affects our whole national economy, so did the fiscal and national policies of the government in power affect agriculture. The greatest hope for Canadian agriculture, and it is often overlooked, is the development of our home markets here in Canada. There is no market in the world that offers more hope for Canadian farmers than our own home market, the home market of your own district, Mr. Chairman, around Orillia, the home markets of our own home counties, the home markets around Kitchener, Waterloo, London, Quebec city, Three Rivers, Brandon, Lethbridge, Vancouver and all the other places.
These home markets are our best markets and have always been our best markets. The minister said this afternoon that he is not going to go out and encourage the production of this or the production of that just because we have too much of something and cannot sell it. I remember when he told people around London a few years ago to get more sows and produce more pigs. They produced more pigs and inside of two years they did not know what to do with the little pigs. He has learned his lesson. No man can be in politics as long as he and I have been without learning something, even though in both cases it might be limited.
I quite agree with that, but I say the government have never had a sound fiscal policy. They have ridden the gravy train for so long that they feel they do not need a policy. They rode into power years ago in the same way, and went out of power after they had lost the world markets. The Minister of Agriculture and his friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce have been in politics a long time, but if they are no longer employed in politics after the next election they had better not hang out their shingles as butter and egg salesmen.
The Minister of Agriculture will say that he has guaranteed a price and that there is not too much butter, but never have we had so much butter in store as we have at the present time. We have more wheat than we have had on any other occasion except one,
Supply-Agriculture
and our surpluses of these products are increasing. We have more or less lost the world markets for these products.
I have listened in the house for many years to chidings, jibes and rumblings from the Liberal party about fiscal policy. They tell us that we must sell if we are going to buy. Well, I have watched the very same party over a quarter of a century selling more and more to the United States of America, where they have ever-increasing surpluses of the very same products to sell.
I have watched the government encouraging that policy. I have watched it all during these years and have read about it in earlier years. We have bought less and less percentagewise from the greatest market for farm products in the world, the British market, and today we have a favourable trade balance with the old land, the British Isles. Last year we had a favourable trade balance. Ever since 1900 we have had a favourable trade balance; down through the years we have accumulated several billions of dollars of favourable trade balances. Yet we are told that the reason we should buy manufactured products from other countries is so we can sell our agricultural products.
From the great republic to the south we are buying the finished products made by their workers who are eating beef produced in the United States and butter and eggs produced in the United States, and who are selling us their finished products to the extent of many billions of dollars. I do not like to repeat figures too often, but this situation has been emphasized in the last few days. Every hon. member is aware of it and I know that the Minister of Agriculture, even though he has more to do than just deal with agriculture, and the other members of the government are properly disturbed at the present time because every day we are buying from the United States almost $3 million more than we are selling to them. Eighty-five per cent of their products are fully manufactured, and their production helps to establish home markets in the United States for the farmers of that country.
I have listened for years and years to people talking about how we are going to solve the problem. I have listened to people say that we must buy where we can buy the cheapest and we must buy if we are going to sell. But, Mr. Chairman, it is very hard to reconcile that as sound fiscal logic if we are going to buy $3 million a day more than we are selling, from the country that has the largest surpluses of what you are trying to sell of any country in the world.
These are the things that are hitting right at the heart of our Canadian agricultural

Supply-Agriculture
prosperity. Our home markets will take our potatoes and our fish from the east. I do not know whether you can call fish an agricultural product altogether, but it does provide work and food for Canadians. Our people will take our dairy products, our poultry and egg products. They will take our beef and pork products and some of that huge surplus of butter the Minister of Agriculture is piling higher and higher. But the government is not giving leadership by way of a sound fiscal policy.
Surely when we are trying to get rid of wheat it is not the time to import United States turkeys into Canada. Three times as many turkeys are coming in now as came in three years ago. Enough turkeys were imported into Canada last year to put almost every turkey man in Canada in the mood to retire from the industry entirely. I have many in my own riding who have written me letters saying they wondered whether the government was going to allow the same thing next year, and if it was they did not think they would continue in the turkey business. You are trying to sell wheat, yet you are importing a million bushels of wheat in the form of turkeys. If all the turkeys consumed in Canada were produced in Canada they would consume at least a million bushels of wheat. Of course, what is a million bushels of wheat to this government? They cannot see the problem because they cannot even see over the piles of wheat.
Why do the government hesitate to do what they have been asked to do by those who understand the industry? Why do you hesitate to put on a tariff of 5 or 10 cents a pound against turkeys coming into this country when the United States, the country that is sending turkeys into Canada as a surplus product produced in a warmer and better climate where it is easier to produce them, put a tariff of 10 cents against the importation of our turkeys? There would be no reflection on you if you recanted. Why do you not drop these old dusty shackles of free trade and do that for these turkey producers even if you will not do it for anybody else?
Why do we need to import cheese from warmer climates where cheese can be produced so much cheaper? I do not know how much is going to come in this year. Three million pounds are sneaked in at one time and five million pounds another time. If you ask about it you are apt to be told it is not in the public interest to give any information, at least until the cheese is eaten. It is like other things. You cannot get any information from the government. Perhaps we would get through the estimates more quickly if we knew something about what is

going on. In all my experience in parliament I have never known a government to sit so quietly and say nothing on everything. However, it is no wonder because the members of the government are always applauded when they refuse to answer.
We have canned meat coming into Canada from countries that can produce meat cheaper than we can. We are even having canned rabbit coming into the country to take the place of beef, the production of which is increasing in Canada.
Yes, Mr. Chairman, it goes far deeper than what you are going to do with a slot-machine policy to try to increase the sale of milk. It goes far deeper than what you are going to do with a wheat policy that has already lost this country hundreds of millions of dollars. It goes far deeper than that. As has been put on Hansard this afternoon, the farmers of almost every country in the world are receiving higher prices for their wheat than is the Canadian farmer. We are told there are millions of people in the world who are starving, yet we have millions of bushels and pounds of surplus foodstuffs in Canada.
It is not my purpose, Mr. Chairman, to hold up this item except to urge the government to look a little further through this haze or maze or cloak of complacency which seems to envelop them, because if they do not that cloak will become their shroud before they are through. Right now we are on the verge of changed conditions in Canada unless we are more careful and give more attention to a sound policy for agriculture. We cannot continue with ever-increasing adverse balances of trade such as we have mounting up at the present time. There is continual harping about the farmers' income dropping 17 per cent in one year, 12 per cent in another year, and so on. Indeed, the farmers' income is down more than the income of any other major branch of Canadian life.
The agricultural industry is not sharing in the increased prices, increased wages and increased general prosperity of the last few years. The fact is that the automobile dealers are beginning to worry; the farm implement dealers are already worried; the farmer himself is worried; the farmer's wife is worried, and the girls and boys going to university are worried because the farmer has these heavy overhead charges and the balance between the cost of production and his sale price is small. He is caught in a squeeze play that is very critical indeed.
I believe that the future of Canadian agriculture, and the future of other industries in Canada, is generally bright, Mr. Chairman, if we have sound fiscal policy. I warn the government that unless it has a change of

attitude, agriculture may face very critical days. You know very well, Mr. Chairman, that if agriculture faces difficult days and this situation grows worse, then the merchant, the manufacturer, the dealer, the labouring man, will feel it just as they have felt it every time agriculture has gone into a recession if not a depression.
I would urge the government to take another look at this adverse balance of trade. In fact they should look at it every night before they go to bed, because it is increasing every day. I say again they should not be ashamed to adopt some of these dusty old theories they had in the past, even if it does mean putting on a protective tariff. We have heard a lot about the tariff on turkeys coming into Canada, on potatoes, on fruits and vegetables. We have heavy investments in all those industries in Canada now. There are people throughout this country today who for 15 years have made the production of turkeys the branch of agriculture upon which they are solely dependent. We have others, many in my own district, who are dependent on fruits and vegetables for their revenue. We have others in the meat business.
The Minister of Agriculture well knows, and I know every hon. member even from the western provinces realizes now as they are diversifying their industry, that mixed farming does help. If we can feed more of our grain to livestock, diversify our whole production and increase our population, thus increasing our home markets, then with sound fiscal policies we will have the best market for agricultural products.
This market has always been the best. The British market has always been the second best. The United States market has always been the most doubtful, the most dangerous and the most unpredictable. The only one in which we are following a practice of buying in order to sell is the United States market, and we are buying more than we are selling. The second best market has been lost, just as it was lost by the same party from 1921 to 1930. The one that is best of all is the one that is least thought of, and the least assisted, because of lack of fiscal policy and unsound general policy dealing with our whole trade situation.

Before the resolution carries there are just one or two remarks I should like to make. First of all, the last speaker suggested the farmers could get out of their difficulty with diversified farming. In general that could be true, but so far as the farmers of my constituency are concerned it could not be done because their farming is of a variety that cannot be alternated year after
Supply-Agriculture
year. Once these trees are planted they are there for 10, 20 or 30 years. The diversification of crops is, therefore, very difficult if not impossible.
The problem of marketing is more intense, in my opinion for the farmers of my constituency than the diversification of their products. I am not going to repeat all that has already been said because the minister has attended conventions, he has received representations and he is fully conversant with the problems affecting the fruit and vegetable growers. I would ask him to pay special attention to the unfair competition these people have suffered for several years. The facts are known to the department. Fruit and vegetable products from the United States are dumped, particularly in the west, at absurd prices just before our own fruits and vegetables are ready for market. This paralyses the market in many cases. Last year potatoes had to be left in the ground because it did not pay to dig them up.
The loss of the United Kingdom market was a severe blow to us. I hope the government will go out of its way this coming year to try to increase the shipments of our fruit to England, particularly apples. I say this because through government assistance we have more and more fruit lands coming into production. These lands were purchased by veterans under the D.V.A. and developed with government assistance. The government therefore has a responsibility to see that the products produced on these government-sponsored lands find a ready market.
My real reason for rising was to express my appreciation of the work done by the experimental farm at Summerland. I spent some time there last summer going through all the various departments and watching them at work, carrying out their operations and trying to solve problems that affect the fruit growers and canners of the valley. I can say this, that I have never come across a staff working so sincerely and earnestly as the staff at that experimental station. I did feel that they were sorely cramped for space. The buildings are old and in many cases obsolete. I understand the government is contemplating erecting new buildings to house at least some of the laboratories and so on.
I hope the minister will tell us later on what is actually being done and when it will be done.
I can assure him that the fruit growers and apple producers of the Okanagan valley are pleased with the work done under cramped conditions at the experimental farm at Summerland. But the loss of the British market created a serious problem in connection with

Supply-Agriculture
our small apples. The British market prefers small apples to any others. Therefore this year we are forced to destroy or get rid of all our Cee grade apples, the 180's in all varieties except Winesaps and New-towns. From now on these apples are to be classified as culls. They are the type of apple they like in Britain because of their small size. In many instances the trees were pruned and planted to grow that type of apple for the old country market. Now these are to be added to the normal culls this coming year, which are culled because of their lack of colour or other blemishes, size development and so on. These small good apples are cull apples now. That is one of the problems with which we have to deal in the Okanagan valley.
There is a limited market for our apple juice, and we have an excellent product which has found a market practically all over North America. The limited outlet for this apple juice does not take care of all the new culls plus the normal culls that will come into the packing houses because of the new ruling. We have also processed some of these apples for pie filler and that kind of thing. It has been done with the help and assistance of the experimental farm, but these outlets do not take care of all our cull apples, and certainly will not this year.
At the convention held in January the British Columbia fruit growers' association passed this resolution:
Be it resolved by this 1956 British Columbia fruit growers' association convention that this association conduct a comprehensive program of research into the possibilities of utilizing apples, particularly into the prospects of developing the making of cider into a subsidiary industry in the Okanagan.
This resolution was carried unanimously. Naturally the farmers are looking to the experimental farm to carry out the necessary experiments to produce a good cider. I have been given to understand that to have a marketable cider it should contain about the same alcoholic content as beer, namely roughly 8 per cent proof and 4 per cent by weight. Then to make it really marketable it has to be clarified and carbonated, and that is where our problem starts.
I am going to suggest to the minister that this is a place where he could combine with the Minister of National Revenue and possibly give some assistance to the farmers. Some 25 or 30 years ago his predecessor in the same office authorized experiments to be carried on at the same experimental station in the making of liqueurs. They produced some excellent brandy and other liqueurs from peaches and apricots. They had a fine still and were doing a remarkable job of research, and everything was ready to be

transferred to commercial use when lo and behold the revenue department came in and smashed the still and all the samples. I hope the minister will not have the same trouble with the present Minister of National Revenue that his predecessor had.
Cider clarified and carbonated calls for an excise tax of $2.50 a gallon. This tax would kill the sale of apple cider, especially in competition with imported wines and so on. To satisfy the revenue department it has to be classified as champagne, of all things; no other wine, just champagne, and that is why it bears that tax per gallon. Without being carbonated it is a dull cider containing only 7 per cent alcohol, less than beer, but it would have to pay an excise tax of 50 cents a gallon. I realize that with this alcoholic content it would have to be sold in liquor stores and beer parlours, which would lower its sale considerably; but at the same time I believe it would afford a wholesome drink in competition with some of the beer that is now being sold.
I have been asked by some of the growers in my riding to make inquiries to see whether the revenue department and the agriculture department could not get together and allow a low grade alcoholic cider to be sold in grocery stores. I do not know whether it is feasible; I am just passing on the suggestion made to me. I have been given to understand that in California, New York and some other states a low alcoholic content cider and other fruit juices are being sold through ordinary grocery and similar channels. The growers who have written to me suggest that something of that kind should be possible in Canada. It would be merely a soft drink made out of apples but presumably it has to contain a small amount of alcohol to keep it from deteriorating, not exceeding 2 to 2J per cent.
I also pass on another suggestion. Commercial alcohol can be made from waste fruit. We have waste fruit that is not even worth putting into cider but it could be made into commercial alcohol, of which a considerable quantity is used in Canada. I have made inquiries to find out where the present alcohol comes from and in what quantities. I find that seven or eight different types of alcohol are brought into Canada each year. Two of the main types can be and are sometimes made from fruit waste. These two types combined amounted to 1,816,949 gallons which we brought into Canada last year, mainly from Germany.
That alcohol could be manufactured from waste fruit products right here in our own country. At Hood River in Oregon there is such a plant that has been operating profitably for many years making commercial

alcohol out of waste fruit. When I made further inquiries as to the possibility of establishing such a plant in the Okanagan valley I found that the first thing you do is to send a bond to the national revenue excise branch for $100,000.
Is that all?

Yes; followed by a licence fee of $250 plus a special type of building erected to their specifications. Then you require a provincial licence as well, so the capital outlay makes it practically impossible to entertain the idea of manufacturing straight commercial alcohol.
Owing to the fact that Canada is dependent on imports of nearly 2 million gallons annually, I would suggest that the department consider carrying on experiments at the experimental farm to find out whether alcohol cannot be produced cheaply by some other means than the expensive way the revenue department demands at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, about a month ago when these estimates first came before the house, I spoke for about four minutes. I waited until the last moment to see whether somebody else would say what I wanted to say and I would not bother rising at all, but there are a few points that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. I should like to tell the minister that I have always held the very highest regard for him because he comes from the county of Huron. He was raised there, and it was too bad that he moved away. I am sorry he went to Saskatchewan, because if there is one thing more than another we do not need it is a Minister of Agriculture from Saskatchewan.
Just to show how discouraged people in other walks of life are with respect to farm prices, may I say that the Ontario provincial chamber of commerce at its annual meeting approved a revised policy for agriculture, stating that international trade has placed many Ontario farmers in a hopeless competitive position. It went on further to state that official announcements on agricultural earnings should be made on a basis of net rather than gross income to avoid erroneous impressions of farm prosperity. The chamber of commerce was disturbed because of the decreased purchasing power of 600,000 farmers across Canada and the decided effect it would have on the economy of the country as a whole.
I think people in all walks of life will agree that as long as agriculture is prospering the rest of the country will share in that prosperity, because agriculturists are the best spenders we have. The labour movement is
Supply-Agriculture
also becoming alarmed at the decline in farm income. They know perfectly well that if their wage rates are to be maintained at the present high levels the farmers must have an increase in income or everyone will suffer. They tell me, as proof that this is true, that Massey-Harris has let out 200 men in Woodstock and Brampton and another 800 in Toronto. That is a total of 1,000 men. If that industry is letting out men surely other industries will begin letting them out before too long, because Massey-Harris is only one of many important industries.
Up to now the general public has not felt the pinch. The farmers are the only group who have not enjoyed the economic boom in this country. I realize that before the minister gets through he will endeavour to tell us how well off they are. He has been telling the farmers that for two or three years, but the fact remains that agricultural income has dropped continuously over the last three years despite what figures the minister may put on the record. It is not good for the farmer or for anyone else, because so many people depend on the farmer. I should like to read an item which appears in an article printed by Free-Market Farming, written by W. M. Curtiss:
The political approach to the solution of farm problems is a proven failure. The way to improve farm income and farm prices is to reduce, not increase, government interference in the pricing and production of farm commodities.
For nearly 30 years, we have tried political schemes of all sorts to solve the farm problem. It is time to try a plan that we know will work- one that has been time tested over nearly a century and a half-a free market for agricultural products.
I know you cannot boost up agriculture with subsidies and then declare it a free market, but the fact remains that as soon as any political group starts interfering with trade they get into trouble. Take the cheese industry for instance. The government tried to market surplus cheese and what happened? The government was not able to do anything. The cheese producer went to work and sold his own products. I do not have the press clipping here, but I read that recently the minister advised the cheese producer to cultivate the home market and not bother with England because it would lower the price of cheese. I thought that was poor advice coming from the minister, because when the government had a chance to sell surplus cheese for Canada the price kept going down until the government could do nothing with it. The cheese producer took over and did a splendid job.
As soon as the cheese producer took over the government brought in six million pounds

Supply-Agriculture
of cheese by way of imports. I do not know for what reason the government did this, unless it was an attempt to discourage the cheese producer altogether. My advice is to leave the cheese producer and the farmer alone and not interfere in any shape, manner or form. They would do better themselves and through the years they have done just that. The principle of supply and demand will look after farm conditions better than any measure of which I have knowledge.
Let us take the sugar beet industry, for instance. We have two sugar beet factories in Ontario, one in Wallaceburg and one in Chatham. Unless the producers get a certain acreage of sugar beets the factories are threatening to close down. The minister knows as well as I that you cannot grow sugar beets without help. The only chance you have of growing them successfully is to have sufficient help to look after the crop. It is not a case of price at all, and that is not the reason for the decreased acreage. They do not have sufficient labour to look after the crop, and unless a change is made the sugar beet factories will have to close down because they cannot carry on. I think it is a pity that this part of our agricultural set-up should cease to exist.
We have a number of Dutch people coming into this country, entire families of them. In many cases they pool their resources and go into the business of growing sugar beets or some other product. Because the whole family is engaged in the business they can take care of the crops, but ordinary farmers have to depend on hired labour. Hired labour is now so expensive that farmers cannot compete, and the result is that they must get out of the Sugar beet business.
Many immigrants come to Canada each year, but they do not stay on the farms for long periods of time. Immigrants came here who were supposed to stay on the farm for at least one year. I tried to tell the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration a few , years ago that this part of the law should be changed. Immigrants should be required to stay on the farm for a period ranging from three to five years. We were getting many immigrants who were not farmers at all. They came to Canada because they thought they could put up with farm life for one year in order to earn their freedom. If they had been required to stay on a farm for three or five years they would not have come to Canada at all, and we would not get that type of immigrant. If a clause were put in the Immigration Act even now which required an immigrant to stay on the farm for at least three years these people would know before

they came here that they were expected to follow the occupation of farming for at least that period of time.
One really cannot expect a man to stay on a farm and work ten or twelve hours a day when he can receive twice as much money in industry for an eight-hour day. That is what happens; the immigrants stay for a month or two and then go off into industry in order to benefit from the high wages.
We have heard quite a lot about turkeys today, and I do not intend to repeat what has been said. I wish to state that I agree with the hon. member for Elgin, who placed some figures on Hansard. I dp not intend to repeat the figures he quoted, but I have one or two points to make.
Why should our turkey producers be subjected to a difference in tariff as between Canada and the United States, and why should the government permit United States turkeys to come to Canada at a lower tariff. I cannot understand why the government would stand by and allow this sort of thing to happen. I hope there will be some correction in that regard. When it is taken up with the cabinet I hope the minister will consider giving the turkey men an even break. They do not want any special consideration; they simply want an even break.
We had a resolution concerning the farm loan act before the house a while ago. I do not intend to speak about that act other than to state a few facts in regard to what, it has had-to do with agriculture. Our difficulty in the past has been that the farmers were not able to get. any money because they had to have such gilt-edged security. The clause which has been put in is simply window dressing, to give the farmers the idea that they are going to receive special consideration.
Those who are administering the act should be permitted to be more flexible and generous with those to whom they are lending money. There is no use putting extra clauses in the .act. There have been no losses for years under this act. The government could not lose money, because farm values have more than doubled. I hope the administrators of the act will take that fact into consideration when they are lending money to farmers who are trying to get along. Some of these farmers are fairly hard up, but they are not so hard up that they would not be capable of paying back a loan. It is not in operations like these that money is lost; money is seldom lost when loaned on farm land. I hope there will be a little more flexibility in the administration of this act. I do not think I shall say anything more at this time, but I may have something to say on particular items.

Mr. Chairman, when I spoke earlier today I found I needed more time than I had, and I have not finished saying what I wanted to say to the committee. I was taking the position that it will be impossible to solve the problems of agriculture in Canada at the present time if we consider them from a short-range point of view without having some system of farm storage for grain and other commodities. The storage charges would be paid to the farmer and the storage facilities would be established on the farm. The farmer would take care of the grain or whatever other commodity is placed in farm storage.
In that way we would be able to take surpluses off the market and we would not have to worry about selling them abroad in competition with the highly subsidized United States exports. At the same time we would be building up a superb supply of different varieties of commodities which we in Canada can produce. These supplies would be of inestimable value in any kind of emergency arising from war or from disaster based upon natural occurrences.
I was naming various commodities which could be stored easily for years. I had dealt with sugar and had pointed out that in southern Alberta alone from High River to the border we could build sugar factories and raise and process sufficient sugar beets to provide two and a half times the amount of sugar consumed annually by all the people in Canada. There are three splendid sugar factories in my constituency, producing in the neighbourhood of 25 per cent of the total Canadian consumption. This sugar could be stored all over the Dominion of Canada so it would be available in case of disaster.
I really fail to see how it is that the Canadian people do not sense this danger and this possibility of overcoming the danger. We hear a great deal about civil defence. Surely the first thing we would need if we were in danger would be food supplies readily available all over the land. We would not want to have to ship wheat from Winnipeg to Edmonton in order that people in Edmonton who may be stricken would be able to live. I maintain that we would be treading upon absolutely sound ground if we had a nationwide system of farm storage for various commodities which we can produce.
I should like to go on to name three or four other commodities which could be stored easily, and then go on to deal with other matters which may have some bearing upon this problem. In this wonderful age in which we live we have learned to dehydrate many of the things we use. The field is almost
Supply-Agriculture
limitless. As everyone knows, we can dehydrate eggs. Milk has been dehydrated with great success, and milk powder can be stored in any dry place and will remain good for I do not know how long, but I imagine for some time. Nothing could be of greater value in time of disaster than plenty of milk powder. Meats can be dehydrated with great success and preserved for a long period of time. Practically every kind of vegetable can be dehydrated, and practically all fruits can be processed in this way with success. All these things could be stored at not too great an expense.
There is no reason why we could not store hay in drier areas like those to be found in certain parts of British Columbia. Great quantities of hay could be stored at not too great an expense. If disaster struck we would need hay for any of the animals that happened to survive. It would be of great value.
Those who are familiar with the beet sugar industry know that in the manufacture of sugar from beets there is a residue called beet pulp which is of great value as a stock food. This beet pulp can be dried and stored in ordinary sacks and shipped to far places to be preserved for an indefinite period of time. It is one of the most nutritious of stock foods. I see no reason why substantial quantities could not be stored in Canada. I would be surprised if similar products could not be made from other root crops. I think that is enough to say about the possibilities in respect of the storing of foods.
Hear, hear.

I know there are always some who will say "Hear, hear" but they would be first to scream in case of disaster. Such people sometimes do not have the intelligence to look beyond the end of their nose.
Now the all-important thing which we are going to have to face is the method of financing. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe spoke about the home market, which he said was the most valuable market for our products. But the home market is no good unless the people in that home market have the dollars with which to buy the commodities that are being offered. Most hon. members, and even the fine hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe with all his experience in this parliament, fail to go beyond the point where they start talking about this matter of finance. That is leaving the job just where it should be begun. He tells us the things we already know and leaves us bewildered regarding all the rest.
This morning I commended the C.C.F. for the very fine showing they made in fighting for the farmer during this last winter, but,

Supply-Agriculture
as I recall it, the C.C.F. said not a single word about what they proposed should be done.
Yes, we did.

I shall leave one of you to say something about it after I have finished. As far as I can recall there was constant complaint against the government for what it had not done. They constantly told how prices should be stabilized and all that kind of thing, once more what everybody in the house and everybody in the country knows.
What they did not say was how the money was going to be obtained to do all this. The only thing the C.C.F. has said, as far as I can recall, is that they can tax the people to get the money. They implied it, although they did not say it. The taxes would begin to fall heavily on the corporations that had been making big profits. I commend the hon. member for Mackenzie for his fine speech, but the only thing he implied was that the big corporations making big profits would be required to share their profits with the government, and from that source we would be able to obtain the funds with which to finance the schemes of the C.C.F.
What is wrong with that?

That is very good. We are in committee, and hon. members can say all they like right after I have finished. I want to put my case, and I am sure they want to put their case, uninterrupted. If they let me put my case so it will be understood, I shall listen most attentively while they put theirs.
As far as the C.C.F. economic proposals are concerned, I oppose them on every point because I believe their whole concept of running a country is fallacious, and if they were able to put their program into operation they would not be able to get the production, much less the distribution.

We are
getting it in Saskatchewan.

Private enterprise is getting it in Saskatchewan. The farmers all over the country, every one of them, constitute private enterprise, and they are simply pouring the wealth out. The same applies to oil or gas developments. You have to have private enterprise come in and do it. If you do not do that you will not get the results. It has been demonstrated beyond a doubt in Alberta. We have invited private enterprise to come in. Then instead of treating it as an enemy whom we wanted to destroy and whom we hated because it made profits, we endeavoured to clear the way

and help private enterprise. As a result we have reaped a rich harvest, and we have a grand prospect of further development just as long as we continue to do so.
In Alberta the private enterprise system is producing abundantly. As I have said many times in this house before, the private enterprise system in America has produced so much that we do not know what to do with it. Our problem now is to learn how to distribute the goods. Certainly in order to distribute the goods it would be most illogical for us to destroy the effectiveness of our productive system. That is exactly what we would do if we began to cultivate the C.C.F. ideas of state socialism, or whatever kind of socialism it is they favour.
So I say that although these people have fought vigorously for the farmer, they have never given us one inkling of what could be done to improve his lot even if they were in charge in Ottawa. The same is true of others. The Conservatives have put up an admirable case for the farmer; I have heard a dozen or more excellent speeches this year from the Conservative benches. But, once more, they have never shown us how the matters were to be remedied financially.
The Liberals this year for the first time have given voice to their ideas, and we have had some very good speeches from Liberals. I have no doubt that if the Liberals were on this side of the house and any one of the parties on this side were over there, the Liberals would be very vocal, energetic and insistent, and still never give any idea as to how to do what they proposed could be done. So I think it is important for us to spend a minute or two on the matter of where we are going to get the money.
This morning, as a result of the announcement that it was proposed that grains and other foods should be shipped to NATO and stored in NATO countries, I asked the question, "Where is anybody going to get the money to buy the goods from Canada and other nations and store them in NATO countries?" Is it proposed that a NATO cabinet should be set up and a NATO premier appointed, and that on top of all the murderous taxes we are enduring in all the countries contributing to NATO we shall have another tax imposed with the object of raising money to buy our goods to store them for NATO? I do not think so. I dealt with that matter this morning to some extent.
If we can manage somehow or other to get money that does not have to be borrowed and paid back, and does not have to be taxed from people, then we can conceive, if we have a sufficient amount of production, how we can do these fine things we want to do for

agriculture; for example, store our grain and pay for it. I draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that under the Finance Act of 1914, the Minister of Finance created in 1917, during the first world war, $50 million Canadian dollars. He did not borrow them from anybody; he created them; and with that money he bought $50 million worth of Canadian produce-wheat, horses and other things which Britain needed in the war. He sent those goods to Great Britain at no cost whatsoever to the Canadian people nor to the British people. Britain in due time repaid the loan, in much the same way as lend-lease operated during the last war, by 1927.
All those who are interested will find an account of this in the report of the royal commission on banking and currency for Canada published in 1933, on page 22, paragraph 47. And right good reading it makes. I would commend that reading to all the members of this house who so earnestly are seeking for a way in which to solve our agricultural problems.
If the minister could create money like that, there is no reason why he could not create money and put it into the hands of the consumers to enable them to buy, and so to realize the home market. There is moreover, no reason in the world why he should not create such money and pay part of the price of the goods, so the consumers could buy, say, a $10 article for $8. When one begins to talk along those lines, he is talking sense. He is talking about something that has been done and could be done, and something that is logical.
One may ask, "How much could he go on printing? $50 billion?" No, he could not, because the limit to the amount he could create is the amount of goods there are in the country to absorb it. The limit is the amount of goods and services there are in the country available for purchase.
That is simple enough for people to understand. There is I repeat no reason why he could not create that money and give a discount on the price of the goods so that, say, a $10 article could be bought for $8. By doing that kind of thing he could increase these home markets, he could utilize them and take advantage of them.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I have listened to the hon. gentleman for perhaps longer than I should without interrupting. I will admit that he is endeavouring to connect his discussion of monetary policy to its effect on agriculture, but I think perhaps the hon. gentleman would be willing to give some weight to the authority I have in my hand, which is entitled, Blackmore's Speaker's Decisions. In it I find several quotations which
