speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION OF ANNUAL HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 211, to provide for annual holidays with pay for employees.
He said: The idea or proposal contained in this bill is not a new one to be suggested on the floor of parliament. However, I think it may be breaking new ground in that, so far as I know, it is the first time an actual bill has been presented to parliament proposing, as this bill does, that by statute all workers in Canada who come under federal labour jurisdiction be given two weeks' holidays per year with pay after one year of employment with their employer.
Hon. members will realize that it is not many decades ago when holidays with pay, particularly for wage earners or industrial workers, were very unusual. I am sure many of us in this chamber have memories-if they are not memories of our own personal experience they are memories of those who have gone before us-of industrial workers or wage earners who never knew during their working lives what it was to have a vacation with pay. True, there were vacations which industrial workers in bygone decades had, but they were vacations due either to illness or to unemployment, and on such occasions there was no remuneration of any kind.
Mr. Speaker, one of the marks of progress of our society is that we have come to recognize, to some extent at least, that all who toil should be entitled to a period of vacation; and it is not a vacation worthy of the name unless one's pay or wage continues during that period. The right to vacations with pay is something for which the trade union movement has fought hard for a great many years. It has carried on that fight at the level of collective bargaining, and many collective agreements in force now between employees and their employers contains provisions for vacations with pay.
These provisions, of course, vary considerably. In some cases the employee gets a vacation with pay after not too long a period of service. In other cases the period of service has to be much longer. The length of the vacation with pay that is provided varies from agreement to agreement. But at any rate, it is fair to say that thanks to the efforts and the struggle of the trade union 67509-243
Industrial Relations
movement, many workers today do enjoy vacations with pay under their collective agreements.
However, with respect to this issue, as with respect to all issues affecting the position of wage earners and industrial workers generally, it has been the feeling and the experience of the trade union movement that a battle of this kind has to be fought on the legislative front as well as at the collective bargaining table. Organized labour, therefore, has sought legislation so that all employees might get at least a certain measure of this right, namely vacations with pay. As a result of these efforts in the legislative field progress has been made in a number of the provinces in this country.
At this point I might remind hon. members that when we are dealing with labour relations in Canada we are dealing with a matter that is under two jurisdictions. There are many employees, indeed most of the industrial workers of this country, who come under provincial jurisdiction. But there are also a large number of workers whose labour relations are under federal labour jurisdiction. Naturally the bill I propose, since it seeks the enactment by this parliament of a federal law, relates only to those who come under federal labour jurisdiction, but I think it is important both as a matter of history and as a basis for my argument that the house should know what progress has been made in the winning of this kind of legislation, and also that the house should know the number of provinces that provide for vacations with pay.
As I say, a number of them have such legislation. I mention first of all, six out of the 10 provinces. These six, if I may name them in geographical order, are Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. There is one other province that has some legislation in this field, and I shall mention it in a moment. The reason I shall mention it separately will be obvious.
First of all may I say with respect to those six provinces on the statute books of which there is legislation compelling employers to grant vacations with pay to their employees, in the case of two of them, namely British Columbia and Saskatchewan, the legislation requires that the vacations with pay be two weeks after one year of service. With respect to the other four provinces, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and Alberta, the requirement is just one week's vacation with pay after one year's service. I should add that in Alberta the law requires that employees be given two weeks vacation with pay after two years of service.
I should also add that in Manitoba the legislation requires that the workers be given two

Industrial Relations
weeks' vacation with pay after three years' service. There are other details that one could spell out, but I think that is sufficient to indicate that some progress is being made in this important and desirable field so far as the wage earners of this country are concerned.
I said that in addition to the six provinces I have named, all of which have vacations with pay legislation which is general in its application in that it applies to all employees in those provinces, it is also to be noted that a seventh province, namely New Brunswick, has a limited provision which gives one week's vacation with pay after one year's employment to those engaged in mining or in construction. It could be that in recent months some changes have been made in some of those provinces, or that other provinces have joined this group; but so far as I can ascertain my information is up to date. Indeed, those who come from British Columbia will recognize that I have included in my information the fact that although British Columbia until recently provided only one week's vacation with pay after one year's service, that province, along with Saskatchewan, now provides by statute two weeks' holidays with pay after one year's service.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this bill obviously seeks to provide under federal law the best of the provisions that already obtain so far as a number of provinces are concerned. This bill, in other words, is somewhat like unto the legislation in the two provinces where they have the best legislation in this field, namely British Columbia and Saskatchewan. I say to any who may study the details of this bill that it is patterned, for the most part, after the legislation in Saskatchewan, although I did take one or two sections out of the new British Columbia bill which it seemed to me it was desirable to include in my proposed bill.
In drafting the bill I drew on the legislation in the two provinces to which I have referred for the general provisions as to vacations with pay. I also drew on certain federal statutes in order to put the bill in proper form. For example, with regard to what employees this legislation might cover, I copied exactly the appropriate section in the legislation known as the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act. That is the section which indicates what employees would be covered, and again it reflects the provisions in this regard which are set out in the British North America Act.
That pretty well indicates what this bill proposes, Mr. Speaker. It proposes that all those employees, all workers, industrial workers, wage earners and others in Canada,

who come under federal labour jurisdiction should now have at least two weeks' vacation with pay each year. It proposes that this should come into effect after one years' employment. There is a provision in the bill to make it clear that this bill supersedes any custom or collective agreement or arrangement that gives to any employees anything less than two weeks' vacation with pay after one year. It also makes it clear that it does not interfere with any custom or collective agreement or other arrangement which gives to any employees anything better than is in this bill.
There is also a provision for prorating the period of vacation with pay that might be given to an employee if he is with an employer for more than one month but for any period less than one year.
Now, Mr. Speaker, other than referring to those details, I do not think I should say too much about the further details of the bill, for two reasons. One, of course, is a very good one in your eyes, namely that on second reading one is not supposed to refer to the sections of a bill. The other is equally good, namely that-I think incidentally this perhaps underlines the reason for that rule-what we are concerned about on second reading is the principle. I invite hon. members to give their attention not so much to the particular details as to how one goes about administering or working out vacations with pay, but rather to the principle that all employees in Canada who come under federal labour jurisdiction should have this right as part of what goes with living in Canada at the present time.
I would point out, sir, since you might be interested in the point, that in my bill I have stayed away from provisions that obtain in some of the provinces such as Manitoba, which involve the government in the selling of stamps, or in any other administrative features that could involve expense. Obviously there is a good reason why I stayed away from those provisions, in order that it would be the kind of bill that a private member might introduce; but even apart from that, I think it is better to have it this way. If the Minister of Labour and his department have studied the bill, as I am sure they have, I hope they may agree with me that it would be better to have it on as simple a basis as possible.
There are in the bill certain provisions for enforcement which involve the minister; but, as I say, the details could be left for further study. My hope is that in this year of 1956 it will not be too hard to persuade the House of Commons of Canada that the workers of Canada should have two weeks' vacation with pay a year, and that the House of Commons

of Canada will therefore approve second reading of this bill; whereupon I, of course, would move not that it go to the committee of the whole right away but rather that it go to the standing committee on industrial relations so that it might be studied very thoroughly in that committee. In the course of that study I would be most happy to accept suggestions from the Minister of Labour, or from anyone else, as to changes in the details. In fact the administrative set-up could be altered considerably and I would not be concerned. My concern, and I think that is obvious, is with the general principle that we should now make it statutory that all employees of Canada under federal labour jurisdiction should have two weeks' vacation with pay.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, in spite of my insistence that what we are dealing with now is the principle, I felt it was incumbent upon me in presenting the bill to the house not to leave the administrative aspect of it in blank form, but rather to show, as I have done in the sections that are in the bill, that such a provision can be worked out and put in practicable form.
As I indicated earlier, Mr. Speaker, organized labour has for years fought hard for this provision. It has carried on that fight at the level of collective bargaining; it has also insisted that gains won at the collective bargaining table should be written into the various statutes of the country. In addition to the fact that the demand for legislation providing for two weeks' vacation with pay after one year was in the platforms of principles of both the former labour congresses of this country, I would point out that it was included in the major 29-point platform of principles which was adopted at the recent founding convention of the Canadian Labour Congress which was held in Toronto during the last week in April. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, what I present to the house at this time is directly in line with the request with this new million-member labour congress, namely national legislation providing for a minimum of two weeks' vacation with pay.
I feel, too Mr. Speaker, that in this matter, as in other matters, the federal parliament of Canada should be giving a lead to the country.
I confess that it is a bit disappointing and a bit frustrating to have to make that plea and feel that so often as far as hon. members opposite are concerned, at least those on the treasury benches, it falls on deaf ears; yet how often we have to do that, particularly in the labour field and in the field of social security, pensions, provision for superannuated civil servants and so on. Every time we argue that the federal government 67509-243i
Industrial Relations
should be a good employer and should be giving a lead, those on the treasury benches sit back as though it was simply their job to follow, as though it were perfectly all right for them to come along with legislation of this kind only when everyone else has it.
I point out, Mr. Speaker, that already some vacations with pay legislation is on the statute books of six-yes, seven-of the provinces of this country. I use the figure seven, including New Brunswick, All these seven provinces have vacations with pay legislation to the extent I outlined a moment ago. I recognize that in the case of only two provinces, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, is that legislation like unto my bill, namely two weeks' after one year. But something is being done in seven out of our ten provinces. I hope we can persuade this House of Commons and the federal government that it is time a lead in this matter was given here.
I know that one of the arguments which will be used-oh, how often we hear it in relation to labour matters-is to leave it to collective bargaining. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is an argument I could go into at length, but I content myself with saying that if the trade union movement thought there was any merit to that argument they would not be bothering with these constant resolutions and platforms of principles calling on legislatures and the parliament of Canada to deal with these matters.
Indeed, if one takes the trouble to look through the 29 points that are in the platform of principles adopted by the Canadian Labour Congress one will find that most of them call for legislation by the federal parliament. One will also find that a great many of these points have been proposed from this corner of the house, in speeches or resolutions or bills such as the one I am presenting at this time.
I earnestly hope that if what I said at the beginning is true, that this is breaking new ground in that it might well be the first time a bill on this subject has been introduced, it will not mean it will have to be shelved for a year or two or five or ten or twenty, as things go around here. Progress has been made in the thinking of people across the years. Progress has been made from the days when an industrial worker worked the whole of his life without ever enjoying a holiday with pay, without ever getting a holiday unless it was due to illness or unemployment. We are proud of the progress that has been made socially in Canada. We are proud of the progress that has been achieved because labour fought persistently for a better deal for the workers of Canada, both organized and unorganized. Indeed, that is one of the reasons that labour advocates

Industrial Relations
legislation in this field; so that the provisions that are won for some by collective bargaining might be won for others, even those outside the ranks of organized labour.
It is an extremely important matter, Mr. Speaker. It is an extremely important item of social progress. No one, not a single hob. member of this house, would stand up and say that industrial employees should not have a vacation with pay every year. Everyone will agree that every employee should have a vacation with pay each year. All right, Mr. Speaker; that being the case, let us say so by supporting the principle of this bill, by voting for it unanimously on second reading and letting it go to the committee on industrial relations for study, whence it can come back to this house to be passed.

speechtext:
Oh, but just in passing. That legislation not only included a provision for vacations with pay but also a provision with regard to hours of work. It is interesting to note the speed with which we have progressed within the last decade, because at that time the reduction of working hours to 48 per week was considered to be a tremendous step forward and was greeted in many quarters with opposition. To introduce legislation today restricting hours of work to 48 hours per week would, I think all hon. members will agree, be greeted with derision from most quarters.
It was in 1936, if my memory serves me well, that the I.L.O. adopted its convention on vacations with pay, and in the meantime a great many countries, whether or not they have implemented the convention, have given it recognition.
In reading the bill which is proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre T was amused to notice the clause which dealt

with notice of the holiday period, not because of the clause itself but because of an amusing story I read quite some time ago. The story concerns a commercial traveller who found himself snowbound in a remote area. He telephoned his employer and asked him for instructions. The employer, who was noted for the tenacity with which he hung on to every dollar, said, "Yes, I have some instructions-start your summer holidays at once." I am sure it is the possibility of such an occurrence which prompted the hon. member to include in his bill the provision which requires at least two weeks' notice of the holiday period.
I must, however, differ with the hon. member when it comes to his comments with regard to the use of stamps or some other such method of determining holiday pay. It has been my opinion that the holiday book and stamp system has worked very well in the province of Ontario. From my perusal of this bill I take it that the employee, upon the termination of his employment with any one employer, would receive at that time the equivalent of the proportion of holiday pay which might be coming to him because of the period of his service.
The situation is a little different in Ontario. The holiday books are purchased and the employer places therein stamps, for which he pays, covering the amount of money owed to the employee on the basis of the vacation. This has the effect that if an employee in the course of a year serves a great many employers-if he is in the type of business, notably the construction business, where he might work for several employers-he might, by keeping this book and having inserted therein the stamps which signify the amount of holiday pay coming to him, accumulate a full holiday pay which he may then procure by turning his book in to any of the banks in the province of Ontario. I do not think this is a very important point, but inasmuch as the hon. member said that he differed with that method of determining the amount due I must say that I agree with the system which has been set up because I know from practical experience the manner in which it has worked.
j must agree with him that the virtue in the legislation is that it covers all workers, whether or not they are members of unions or negotiating groups. The main argument against leaving arrangements of this sort to negotiating bodies is that those workers who are not unionized are left out and do not enjoy the privileges which may be extended to those who belong to unions.
I think we all agree that everyone deserves a holiday after working a year, though probably a good many of us in this house have not had as many as we should have had in

the years we have been here. Working conditions improve as the years go by and they improve because of the interest not only of labour organizations, which deserve a large share of the credit, but of legislators who interest themselves in the conditions under which the people of this country labour.
For all these reasons I propose to support this bill. I know that my support will be echoed by my leader, who is unavoidably absent at this time. I know that if he were here he would have some remarks to make on this legislation, because it would bring back to his mind the period when he was premier of Ontario and so keenly interested in the plight of the workers in his province, and the extent to which he promoted progressive labour legislation in that province.

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: PROVISION OF ANNUAL HOLIDAYS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have read this bill with great interest, and again it indicates the well known diligence of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He stated in his remarks that he believed this was the first round in so far as the federal ring is concerned, and I think that is true.
Both he and the hon. member for Hamilton West referred to the fact that in the earlier part of this century vacations with pay were a matter which did not receive anything like the consideration and interest which has developed since the end of the last great war. Certainly there were vacations, but too often they were vacations without pay or without any sign of employment to call a halt to the vacation. It was those long series of forced unpaid vacations which led the federal government to request that the British North America Act be amended in order that there might be something in the way of a backlog during these unpaid vacations which would offset the hardship imposed.
I do not think anyone will disagree with the principle that all who toil hard and consistently are entitled to vacations, and that if conditions warrant those vacations should be paid for. At the same time I think all of us should realize that paid vacations must be related to many other factors which enter into arrangements between employer and employee. For instance, there is the number of statutory holidays to be allowed and the number to be paid for, there is the length of the working week and how many days in the week are to be paid for, there is the amount of overtime to be worked and the payment for same, and half a dozen other factors that could be listed.
As I said, Bill No. 211 brings before the house for the first time some interesting questions for debate. I hope the debate will be full because I am sure it will be profitable.
Industrial Relations
The bill proposes that all employees in Canada who come under federal labour jurisdiction shall be granted at least two weeks' holidays with pay after one full year of employment.
For a number of years before the last war we had legislation providing for the settlement of disputes in industries under federal jurisdiction, and since 1948 we have had the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act which replaced the former legislation. That act covered the regulation of some collective bargaining aspects of labour relations as well as dealing with the all-important matter of providing the means or technique for the settlement of labour disputes.
Since I became Minister of Labour in 1953 we have brought in two additional measures. One was the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act, which prohibits discrimination in employment because of race, colour, national origin, religion or creed. At this session there is to be introduced legislation to provide equal pay for female employees as compared with male employees. But I think Bill No. 211 differs from those two measures in that it proposes to set a specific minimum standard in respect to one aspect of working conditions, namely annual vacations with pay. That fact makes it somewhat different from the legislation I have mentioned.
Federal industries are of course those works, businesses and undertakings which come under federal jurisdiction, and in spelling these out in the act my hon. friend has very kindly used the language of the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act.

If you will just take the

speechtext:
The validity of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, which is applicable to the federal industries listed in the bill, came before the Supreme Court of Canada only last year and was upheld in a judgment given on June 28, 1955. Perhaps I should run over the industries listed in order to make the record complete. They include transportation and communications, including railways, shipping and stevedoring; air transport; international trucking and bus lines; telegraphs; telephones in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia; broadcasting; terminal elevators and the processing of western grain; banks, and grain companies.
The total number of employees in these industries is just under 400,000, which is not a large proportion of the roughly 5,000,000 paid workers we have in Canada. As federal Minister of Labour I recall that figure from time to time with a great deal of satisfaction, because within 400,000 workers there cannot be nearly as many labour disputes as might be involved in the several million workers.

Industrial Relations
Employees in those industries, taking them as a whole, are much more highly organized than employees generally, and about 70 per cent of them have their conditions of employment set already by collective agreements, as compared with 39 per cent for all the other industries in Canada, which come under the provincial jurisdiction. If, then, parliament should indicate a specific minimum standard in respect of a matter such as annual vacations, it will be passing a law on a subject which is normally dealt with by collective bargaining for a large proportion of the employees affected.
In spite of the comment by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre on that factor being brought up from time to time, nevertheless I believe it is an important factor for any federal minister of labour in approaching a measure such as this.
Legislative standards on matters normally dealt with by collective bargaining may sometimes be necessary, usually as a means of ensuring that unorganized workers are not deprived of all the protection they should have. I am sure in the great industrial province of Ontario that was certainly one of the factors responsible for the legislation in 1944. But I am sure that as members of the federal parliament we would want to move with a certain caution, particularly when a large proportion of the employees under federal jurisdiction have established these standards by the process of collective bargaining.
In the present instance the question arises as to how adequately the employees affected are already assured of paid vacations after one year's full work. A recent estimate of the number of workers under federal jurisdiction was, as I said, just under 400,000, of whom 47 per cent now meet the standard sought to be established by this bill. An additional 2 per cent qualify for two weeks' vacation after two years' service, an additional 44 per cent after three years' service, and an additional 1 per cent after five or more years' service.
Therefore less than 1 per cent of employees under federal jurisdiction are known not to receive two weeks' vacation at any time, while for the remaining 6 per cent, for the most part in the stevedoring industry, the information available is not sufficient to determine the length of their annual vacations.
Mr. Speaker, I have done some homework putting this out in chart form, and I should be very glad to give it to the house. The chart is headed "Estimated distribution of employees under federal jurisdiction according to service required for two weeks' vacation with pay". The subheadings across the top are, first, "Industry", giving the industries under federal jurisdiction; next "Coverage",
iMr. Gregg.]
giving the total number covered; then "Service requirement for two weeks' vacation", with subcolumns for one year, two years, three years, five years and more than five years. The next column is headed "Do not get two weeks' vacation"; the final column is headed "No information". Under each heading there are two columns, one giving the number and the other the percentage. I can give a few of the headings to the house now if hon. members would like to have them.
For the steam railways, including telegraph operations, the total number is 196,800. The number with one year's service is 44,900 or 22-8 per cent. There is nothing listed for two years' service. The number for three years is 151,900, and that is 77-2 per cent. There are none for five years or more than five years.
For shipping, including stevedoring, the total is 34,200. With one year's service, 12,200 or 35-7 per cent; with two years' service, 1,400 or 4-1 per cent; with three years, 1,500 or 4-4 per cent; with five years, 1,600 or 4-7 per cent. There seems to be no doubt that in the last ten years there has been a steady trend toward longer vacations after shorter periods of service in industry generally, and particularly in the federal industries. As a matter of fact this very item is a most important one in the agreements that are being reviewed in Montreal this very day. I think we must consider this trend in determining whether there is any real need for federal legislation on this matter. It seems to me also that there are other implications to be considered in setting specific standards for working conditions in our federal industries.
Where working conditions for a large proportion of employees in any jurisdiction, are already established by collective bargaining, it could very well be that standardization through legislation is not desirable. When working conditions are left to collective

bargaining there is the ability to inject into them a flexibility in determining standards which is lacking when any government introduces minimum standards. In some instances an increase in wages or salaries or an improvement in some one or more fringe benefits may be more acceptable to the employees than a longer paid vacation leave. I am sure one can let his imagination run and realize how that could happen. I should like to emphasize also that it is not only the length of the paid vacation that such legislation would standardize but a number of other important conditions relating to it.
If a vacation pay law is to deal clearly with the ancillary matters which frequently arise in the administration of a vacation plan, it would have to cover such factors as (1) length of service required to qualify for

vacation privileges; (2) the effect of interruptions of service on such privileges; (3) the methods of determining vacation pay, for example, a percentage or proportion of normal weekly earnings or average weekly earnings;
(4)	the time when the vacation is to be taken;
(5)	whether or not vacations are to be termed an accrued monetary right so that an employee who terminates his employment before taking his vacation is to receive pay in lieu of such vacation. One could go on and name others which are not as important as those I have named.
The bill before the house deals with some of these points, and there are probably others that would need to be taken care of by legislation. Legislation means standardizing practice in all these particulars as well as the length of the vacation, and the arbitrary rules that would have to be set in the legislation might not be as acceptable to the employees concerned as the freely negotiated rules they have worked out with their employers by collective bargaining. This would be particularly true in industries such as shipping and longshoring, where vacation benefit arrangements peculiar to the conditions in those industries are now in effect and are only in effect after a great deal of study and arrangement between the two parties concerned.
Another point I wish to make is the difficulty of arriving at a minimum standard if one is to be set. As I have already indicated, there is considerable variation in the federal jurisdiction both in the practice that has been established in industries where collective agreements govern conditions of employment and in others where vacations with pay plans are part of the personnel policy of the employer.
I have here a summary of what is happening in the various provinces of Canada. That has been summarized by both hon. members who have preceded me. I think I have one or two slight variations from what was set out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and if I were to put what I have on Hansard perhaps it would be a matter of controversy.
